Ripple CEO Brad Garlinghouse noted on Nov. 19 that crypto markets could rally after Anthropic's IPO, as they did after SpaceX went public. He spoke to CNBC on the day Anthropic's shares started trading on Nasdaq under the ticker ANT.

According to Garlinghouse, investors sold Bitcoin and XRP before the listing to free up cash for shares of the Claude developer.

In a recent development, "We talked earlier about the most recent sell-off in the crypto markets — we also saw a sell-off very similar when SpaceX went public. What happens is you've got risk-on assets and people are taking liquidity out of a very liquid market, crypto included — Bitcoin, XRP — and moving it into SpaceX. The exact same thing happened coming into the Anthropic IPO. What we saw after the SpaceX IPO was a rally in the crypto markets. I think you'll see that happen here as well," the Ripple CEO remarked.

Recent findings suggest that anthropic priced its IPO at $83 per share, above the initial range of $70 to $78. The manufacturer and its seven co-founders sold 980 million shares, up from the 825 million shares they planned to sell earlier. The offering raised $81.3 billion, and a $26 billion private placement brought the total to $107.3 billion.

Industry observers note that at a valuation of about $1.5 trillion, Anthropic became the world's 12th-biggest tech giant, just behind Tesla. SpaceX raised $75 billion in its market debut in June.

According to recent reports, dan Ives of Yorkville Ives said that "Anthropic's IPO is a massive near-term win for the tech sector." University of Florida finance professor Jay Ritter compared AI with the early internet. "Thirty years ago, the internet was the next big thing. It has changed our lives. Today, artificial intelligence is the next big thing. It will change our lives, too," Ritter said.

According to recent reports, asked about the listing itself, Garlinghouse stated that Anthropic's shares would trade well. "I think it's gonna be extremely well received, and we obviously saw a price above the range they had. I think it's gonna trade very well," he said.

In the same interview, Garlinghouse called blockchain-based transactions "a wave of emerging technology." "I think 10 years from now you'll see blockchain implemented across our financial infrastructure," he remarked.

After the SpaceX IPO in June, Bitcoin took almost three weeks to turn higher. It started to rise after the U.S. Treasury announced that it would buy back government bonds.

Tech Report: Exchange Ledgers in the Middle as CFTC and SEC Diverge on What “Delivery” Means

📅 30 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1262 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, A customer buys a token on a U.S.
  • Under the SEC's crypto proposal, delivery doesn't decide the question at all.
  • Open almost any crypto exchange app after a purchase and you'll see a clean number: 1.0000 ETH, available.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

In a recent development, A customer buys a token on a U.S. exchange and the app shows the balance. Under the CFTC's December 14 framework, nothing has been delivered yet.

Under the SEC's crypto proposal, delivery doesn't decide the question at all. An October 27 comment letter asks the two agencies to settle on one answer.

Open almost any crypto exchange app after a purchase and you'll see a clean number: 1.0000 ETH, available. To the customer, the asset is theirs. To the exchange's database, it's a row in an internal ledger. To federal regulators, that row is now being judged by two different tests that don't agree on what it means.

According to recent reports, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) has opened an advance notice of proposed rulemaking on what it calls Regulation Crypto Asset Transactions (CTX) and Regulation Crypto Asset Markets (CAM). It sets out the agency's first formal view of "actual delivery" for crypto since it withdrew its 2020 guidance last December. Comments close on December 14.

The Securities and Exchange Commission's Regulation Crypto Assets proposal takes a different view of the same moment. Then, on October 27, a comment letter on the SEC's file raised the gap directly. It described the situation as "two conflicting definitions of the same physical facts" and asked the agencies to "please coordinate the definitions.".

Delivery matters because it decides which rulebook applies.

Sources indicate that for the CFTC, the answer comes from Section 2(c)(2)(D) of the Commodity Exchange Act. A leveraged, margined or financed retail commodity trade is treated like a futures contract unless "actual delivery" happens within 28 days. If delivery happens in time, the trade falls outside futures rules. If it doesn't, the exchange is effectively running a futures venue.

It has been revealed that for the SEC, the question is whether a token is still part of an investment contract. Under the August proposal, a covered investment contract ends when the issuer has finished or permanently stopped its essential managerial efforts and files a Form TR transition report. Whether the buyer has received the token is not part of that test.

So one agency treats delivery as the deciding question, and the other barely considers it.

According to recent reports, the CFTC's position is still preliminary, but it is detailed. Published in the Federal Register on October 13, the notice relies on the Monex case standard: actual delivery requires "the transfer of some meaningful degree of possession or control.".

For crypto, the agency suggests that possession and control "may require possession of the credentials (e.g., private key(s))." It takes three positions that matter most to exchanges:.

The agency is also asking whether control has to be exclusive, whether delivery can happen while a lien or security interest is outstanding, and how financing offered in an exchange's standard account documents affects whether a trade is covered at all.

Recent findings suggest that the SEC's proposal, released on August 18, deals with a different question. It creates offering exemptions, including a $5 million startup exemption over four years, and a safe harbor for when a crypto asset's investment contract ends. Neither depends on where the token sits.

Under the proposal, a token held in a customer's self-custody wallet and a token recorded on an exchange's books are treated the same way. In both cases, the investment contract question depends on the issuer's managerial efforts and its filings.

Sources indicate that that is the gap the October 27 letter tries to close. Its author, who describes themselves as a fintech founder designing a consumer platform, argues that "where the customer holds the private keys or execution is on-chain, with custody evidence, the asset should be treated as delivered and the covered-investment-contract analysis should end there.".

Running four common exchange transactions through both frameworks highlights where the tests split.

Trade one: a fully paid purchase left on the exchange.

Trade two: the same purchase withdrawn to a self-custody wallet on day three.

Trade three: a margined purchase kept on the exchange's ledger for 30 days.

Trade four: an on-chain swap that settles directly into the user's wallet.

Industry observers note that the pattern is consistent. Self-custody is the only position that clearly counts as delivery under the CFTC's view and also ends the analysis under the letter's proposed SEC fix. Everything left on an exchange's internal ledger stays in an unclear position. The CFTC treats it as undelivered and the SEC's text doesn't address it.

In a recent development, the letter was filed on October 27, a week after the SEC's October 20 comment deadline. It is anonymous and brief, but its main concern is practical. If the definitions stay separate, it warns, founders will have to design products around whichever rule is stricter.

It is the only filing on either docket so far that sets the two definitions side by side.

Sources indicate that the CFTC process is still at the advance-notice stage, so a formal proposal will follow. For U.S. platforms, though, the direction is clear. Under the CFTC's preliminary reading, an exchange that keeps customer assets in internal ledger accounts has not delivered them. If that exchange also offers margin or financing, it is on track to be treated as a futures venue.

The SEC's final rule could adopt the letter's custody-based approach or keep delivery out of its analysis entirely. Until one of those happens, the same ledger entry can be undelivered for one regulator and irrelevant for the other.

Recent findings suggest that exchanges and their customers have until December 14 to say which definition should prevail. The real decision is whether "delivered" ends up meaning the same thing at both agencies.

Amazon acquires key assets of AI startup Decart for reported $7.5B

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (828 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • today declared plans to hire the technical staff of startup Decart.AI Inc.
  • In a recent development, the organization didn’t disclose the terms of the deal.
  • In August, reports emerged that the tech giant had drawn takeover interest from Anthropic PBC.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 20:40 EST / NOVEMBER 23 2026.

Amazon.com Inc. today declared plans to hire the technical staff of startup Decart.AI Inc. and acquire its core technology.

In a recent development, the organization didn’t disclose the terms of the deal. However, sources told Bloomberg that Amazon is paying about $7.5 billion. That’s nearly twice the valuation Decart reportedly received after its most recent funding round in May.

In August, reports emerged that the tech giant had drawn takeover interest from Anthropic PBC. The artificial intelligence provider reportedly sought to buy Decart for $6 billion but walked away from the deal in September. Rumors that Amazon could swoop in emerged the following month.

Industry observers note that decart founders Dean Leitersdorf, Moshe Shalev and Orian Leitersdorf will join the tech giant along with Decart’s research team. Additionally, Amazon is acquiring the technology behind the firm’s DOS platform, which helps boost the efficiency of AI models. Decart claims that the software can reduce the cost of some neural networks by a hundredfold.

Recent findings suggest that the manufacturer hasn’t shared detailed information about how DOS works. However, the blog post in which Decart revealed its May funding round did reveal that the platform optimizes AI models by “tuning the kernels.”.

Kernels are the basic building blocks of neural networks. They’re relatively simple code snippets designed to run across a large number of chip cores. One common approach to optimizing them, kernel fusion, combines multiple kernels into a single code snippet that uses less hardware. In July, Decart disclosed that a custom model it had developed with DOS uses kernel fusion.

Sources indicate that the organization states that the platform also includes “proprietary compilers.” AI compilers translate neural networks into the platform-specific programming language of the host chip. They also optimize the models along they way. For example, the compiler that Amazon Web Services offers for its AWS Trainium machine learning chip uses quantization to compress models into a more memory-efficient form.

It’s unclear whether Decart positions DOS as an alternative to the default compilers provided with AI accelerators. According to Amazon, Decart has “worked closely” with its engineers since 2025 to optimize the performance of workloads deployed on its Trainium chips. The newest commercially available iteration of the chip, Tranium3, provides 2.52 petaflops of performance when processing FP8 data.

Amazon stated that the acquisition will help “further optimize both its inference and custom silicon performance.” According to the organization, the goal is to not only speed up customers’ models but also lower their cost.

Sources indicate that “Every leap forward in AI starts with getting more out of every chip,” said Peter DeSantis, Amazon’s senior vice president of foundational AI models, custom silicon and quantum computing. “More efficient compute means better training, better reinforcement learning, faster inference, and better models for customers at a lower cost.”.

Industry observers note that the acquisition doesn’t include Decart’s portfolio of internally developed AI models. Its two newest algorithms, Lucy 2.5 and Oasis 3, are world models that generate virtual environments based on prompts. The former algorithm is optimized for low-latency content creation, while the latter is designed to generate training data for robots.

Latest findings point to fuel supply, not Blue Origin’s engines, in loss of Amazon Leo satellites

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (365 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Geekwire

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 18, 2026 at 10:01 amNovember 18, 2026 at 10:08 am.
  • Blue Origin’s engines look like they’re off the hook, at least for now.
  • In a recent development, the two BE-4 engines Blue Origin makes for United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket weren’t to blame for the low thrust in Sunday’s failed launch, according to preliminary findings released Wednesday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 18, 2026 at 10:01 amNovember 18, 2026 at 10:08 am.

Blue Origin’s engines look like they’re off the hook, at least for now.

In a recent development, the two BE-4 engines Blue Origin makes for United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket weren’t to blame for the low thrust in Sunday’s failed launch, according to preliminary findings released Wednesday. Instead, it appears the engines didn’t get enough fuel from the rocket, ULA said.

In its latest patch on the investigation, ULA mentioned it had completed an initial integrated review of flight data. Preliminary data indicate the first stage’s low thrust came from “inadequate fuel supply from the vehicle to the BE-4 engines, not from the performance of the engines,” ULA said, adding that work remains to determine the cause.

In a recent development, on Tuesday, ULA mentioned early data suggested the first stage underperformed just after liftoff, leaving the rocket too low and too slow to put 40 of Amazon’s Leo internet satellites into orbit. It didn’t say then whether the engines played a role.

It has been revealed that the BE-4s are made by Jeff Bezos’ Kent, Wash.-based Blue Origin. Blue Origin CEO Dave Limp mentioned Wednesday on X that he was proud of the BE-4 team for its “rapid response and support of ULA’s investigation” and that the organization looks forward to Vulcan’s return to flight.

Sources indicate that the finding matters for Blue Origin beyond Vulcan. Its own Upcoming Glenn rocket uses seven BE-4s on its first stage, and Amazon has 24 New Glenn launches reserved for Leo.

ULA repeated that Vulcan’s second stage appears to have started normally and that its RL10 engines operated as planned but couldn’t make up for the earlier loss of performance. The six Northrop Grumman solid rocket boosters, the source of problems on two earlier Vulcan flights, appear to have performed normally, ULA stated.

In a recent development, the Federal Aviation Administration is overseeing the ULA-led investigation. Amazon’s next Leo launch is an Ariane 6 mission carrying 36 satellites, targeted for no earlier than Nov. 23 from French Guiana.

ULA said it will share more as the investigation continues.

  • The data reveals that Bitcoin's apparent demand is rapidly showing signs of weakness, with the metric dropping below -290,000 BTC before seeing a brief recovery to about -255,000 BTC as of November 18.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bitcoin is facing increased fear and panic among traders as its price volatility continues to intensify, causing both retail and institutional investors to move with caution.

While Bitcoin is still struggling to regain momentum amid the persistent market downturn, the latest on-chain data from CryptoQuant shows that Bitcoin's demand has dropped to its weakest level in 2026.

The data reveals that Bitcoin's apparent demand is rapidly showing signs of weakness, with the metric dropping below -290,000 BTC before seeing a brief recovery to about -255,000 BTC as of November 18.

However, this does not provide any relief, as Bitcoin’s apparent demand remains substantially below its monthly average of around -172,000 BTC.

Industry observers note that as such, it appears that investors’ interest in accumulating Bitcoin remains significantly subdued by the fear of potential losses. Hence, investors are growing increasingly cautious about entering the market amid the rising selling pressure.

The data demonstrates that investors are growing increasingly wary of their Bitcoin positions amid growing uncertainty about its potential price movements, as Bitcoin’s price downturn has only intensified over the past few days.

While the asset’s price has dipped further, Bitcoin has suddenly retested $62,000 as of November 18, a price level last seen during the severe price crash in July.

Nonetheless, further data indicates that it has briefly recovered to $63,817.43 as of the time of writing, showing a decline of about 1.12% over the past 24 hours.

Despite Bitcoin’s extremely negative demand and weak price movements, market analysts are still positive about a potential reversal, describing the moment as an opportunity to buy at a lower price.

It has been previously observed that while many investors are becoming increasingly bearish, periods of widespread fear can sometimes flush out weaker hands, thereby triggering a change in market direction.

Industry News: AI startups feared Nvidia’s money would dry up without Jensen Huang. His return as CEO has put those fears to rest

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (681 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fortune

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Jensen Huang is back as Nvidia CEO after just shy of two weeks of turmoil.
  • Nvidia has become what some have referred to as the “central bank of AI.” The tech giant has invested in and supplied compute to various AI startups, neoclouds, and AI labs.
  • It has been revealed that indeed as of the end of July, Nvidia had invested nearly $50 billion in AI model makers such as OpenAI, Anthropic, and xAI, and its equity stakes across the AI ecosystem totaled twice that.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jensen Huang is back as Nvidia CEO after just shy of two weeks of turmoil. The news—which has come as a shock to many in the tech world—was a welcome relief to investors and Nvidia’s partners, who had spent the majority of that time fretting that the organization’s financial commitments might dry up.

Nvidia has become what some have referred to as the “central bank of AI.” The tech giant has invested in and supplied compute to various AI startups, neoclouds, and AI labs. These companies then, in part, use that money to buy Nvidia chips. Critics have called this process “circular financing,” with many saying it leaves much of the AI boom dangerously exposed to weak links.

It has been revealed that indeed as of the end of July, Nvidia had invested nearly $50 billion in AI model makers such as OpenAI, Anthropic, and xAI, and its equity stakes across the AI ecosystem totaled twice that. It has also pledged $170 billion of its investment-grade credit to help AI companies and neoclouds get financing.

According to recent reports, before news of Huang’s reinstatement broke on Monday, several investors and Nvidia partners told Fortune they were concerned that these commitments might stall under the interim CEO. That interim CEO, Colette Kress, some said, already showed early signs of being more hesitant to make deals at the same rate as Huang. Any newly introduced CEO, they added, would likely want to appear as a steady hand and more cautious when it came to spending.

“Jensen has been such a critical part of the ecosystem because he’s allowed Nvidia to provide compute to venture stage companies who otherwise don’t have access to it,” stated one investor who asked to be anonymous to discuss private deals. “Everyone was concerned about whether the next person at the helm of Nvidia would also be as aggressive in fostering that ecosystem.”.

For a while, the investor said, any startup that landed a meeting with Huang was likely to walk away with funding.

There were also worries about commitments to so-called neoclouds, such as CoreWeave or Nscale. These companies buy Nvidia GPUs, often with large amounts of debt, and rent the computing power to AI labs, startups, and enterprises. Nvidia has taken equity stakes in some of them and guarantees some of their data center leases. It has also agreed to rent back unused capacity at a fixed rate, which gives banks a floor that makes them more willing to lend. For example, Nvidia has agreed to buy up to $6.3 billion of CoreWeave’s unsold capacity through 2032.

If Nvidia pulled back on some of these investments, the neoclouds most exposed would be those selling capacity to buyers without investment-grade credit, since they might not be able to finance GPUs without a backstop. This could have the knock-on effect of slowing some latest data center projects.

In a recent development, huang’s personal touch extended to Nvidia’s supply chain, too. After his resignation, Elon Musk wrote on X that many of Nvidia’s critical deals were “a handshake with Jensen” and warned that “at least some of those critical deals will be lost” without him.

In a recent development, with Huang back at the helm, investors expect Nvidia to keep acting as the AI industry’s lender; AI startups, labs, and neoclouds that lean on Nvidia for funding, compute, and credit backstops have more reason to expect those deals will keep coming at the pace they’d grown used to. The market seemed to agree, with Nvidia shares jumping more than 30% on Monday, and analysts at Melius Research and Bernstein swiftly upgrading the stock.

Industry observers note that “Jensen Huang’s return is an enormous positive for Nvidia and the broader AI trade, removing a major source of uncertainty and restoring the visionary leadership that helped build the entire AI infrastructure ecosystem,” remarked David Miller, CIO at Catalyst Funds. “While questions remain about the ultimate returns on massive AI capital expenditures, today’s announcement meaningfully improves sentiment and reduces a major risk that had been hanging over the sector.”.

Tech Report: Clock Ticking on Zcash’s Sprout Pool: 22,263 ZEC Unmoved Ahead of NU7 Lock

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Daily pool data shows Sprout holders moved more than 300 ZEC out in a September rush, then almost stopped.
  • Unless someone acts in the next few days, nearly all of what remains will be unspendable at block 3,543,405.
  • Recent findings suggest that most coverage of Zcash's upcoming Sprout freeze quotes the same figure, about 22,000 ZEC.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Daily pool data shows Sprout holders moved more than 300 ZEC out in a September rush, then almost stopped. The last withdrawal was on October 19.

Unless someone acts in the next few days, nearly all of what remains will be unspendable at block 3,543,405.

Recent findings suggest that most coverage of Zcash's upcoming Sprout freeze quotes the same figure, about 22,000 ZEC. That number is accurate, but it is a single snapshot. It doesn't show whether the people who own those coins are doing anything about the deadline.

We checked the pool every day, and the answer so far is no.

In a recent development, according to ZecStats' daily value-pool records, Sprout has held exactly 22,263.34162335 ZEC since October 19. That is 11 straight days, and more than 12,000 blocks, without a single zatoshi leaving the pool. Our October 25 piece recorded the drop from 22,309 ZEC to 22,263 ZEC. Since then the balance hasn't moved.

According to recent reports, zecStats publishes a daily CSV of every Zcash value pool, using the last block of each UTC day. Its figures follow the valuePools field that a full node returns through the getblockchaininfo call. The archive starts on July 30, 2026, and gives a 92-day picture of the Sprout pool.

Across those 92 days, about 374 ZEC, or 1.65% of the pool, left Sprout. That is an average of roughly 4 ZEC a day. The average hides the real pattern, though: the pool moved on only 15 of the 92 days.

Most of the withdrawals came in a few large transfers in September:.

Industry observers note that together with smaller moves on August 31, September 17 and September 19, the 30 days to September 29 saw 310.5 ZEC leave Sprout. That is about 10 ZEC a day.

According to recent reports, october was much quieter. Apart from one withdrawal of 46.05 ZEC on October 19, the month's activity was small change:.

Since October 19, there has been no movement at all.

It has been revealed that at September's pace, about 70 ZEC more would leave before activation. At October's pace, it would be well under 15 ZEC. On the last 11 days' pace, the answer is zero.

The deadline is set in ZIP 259, which defines how the NU7 network upgrade is deployed. It sets the mainnet activation height at 3,543,405.

It has been revealed that NU7 does not introduce a new transaction format. Instead, after activation, version 4 transactions become invalid, while versions 5 and 6 remain valid. Sprout's design is the problem. As ZIP 259 puts it: "Because Sprout transfers can only be represented by version 4 transactions, funds remaining in the Sprout pool become unspendable.".

According to recent reports, the coins would not be destroyed, and NU7 does not change Zcash's supply cap. They would simply be stuck in a pool that no valid transaction can spend from. Today the stranded amount would be 22,263 ZEC, about 0.13% of the roughly 17.01 million ZEC in circulation.

The rest of the upgrade is larger:.

ZIP 259 also skips Zcash's usual three-month gap between the first supporting software release and activation. Operators running unsupported software could stay online and follow a pre-NU7 chain.

Industry observers note that as of ZecStats' latest upgrade on October 30 at 13:09 UTC, the chain was at block 3,535,877. That leaves 7,528 blocks until activation.

According to recent reports, in October, the network averaged about 1,147 blocks a day, or one roughly every 75.3 seconds. At that rate, block 3,543,405 arrives around 02:00–03:00 UTC on November 6. That is the evening of November 5 in the Americas and the early hours of November 6 in Europe and Africa.

Small changes in block times could move that window by a few hours. Holders who initiative to move funds on the final day risk missing the cutoff.

In practice, getting funds out of Sprout means sending a version 4 transaction that moves them into a newer pool before activation. Consumers need software that can still build Sprout transactions and a synced node or wallet that recognizes their old notes.

Industry observers note that the September withdrawals show that some holders are still paying attention. Several were round amounts, such as 99.998 ZEC, which is consistent with someone moving 100 ZEC and paying a fee. The 11-day pause since October 19 suggests something else: most of the remaining 22,263 ZEC may belong to keys that are lost, forgotten or no longer used.

It has been revealed that that has been part of the debate about Sprout for years. A pool that has been shrinking slowly since Zcash's early days is now on a fixed timetable. The daily data indicates that most of its remaining balance is not being moved.

Sources indicate that every report that cites "about 22,000 ZEC at risk" is technically correct. The more useful figure for anyone tracking the upgrade is the rate of change, and right now that rate is zero.

The useful thing to watch over the next week is whether the Sprout line in ZecStats' daily data moves again before block 3,543,405. If it doesn't, Zcash will activate NU7 with about 22,263 ZEC permanently locked in its first shielded pool. That would be one of the largest deliberate freezes of user funds by any major blockchain upgrade, and nearly all of it would be coins whose owners did not move them in time.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • On this day, 17 years ago, Satoshi Nakamoto opened an account on BitcoinTalk, the place that would become the home of early Bitcoin enthusiasts and then turn into a public forum for crypto in general, until social media platforms took over the internet.
  • The network itself was barely 1 year old, and its future raised more questions than answers.
  • In a recent development, in 2010, the revolution began: 10,000 BTC was used to buy two pizzas, one of the first uses of the digital asset in exchange for a commodity.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On this day, 17 years ago, Satoshi Nakamoto opened an account on BitcoinTalk, the place that would become the home of early Bitcoin enthusiasts and then turn into a public forum for crypto in general, until social media platforms took over the internet.

The network itself was barely 1 year old, and its future raised more questions than answers. Satoshi Nakamoto welcomed people on the forum and invited any questions people had regarding the cryptocurrency.

In a recent development, in 2010, the revolution began: 10,000 BTC was used to buy two pizzas, one of the first uses of the digital asset in exchange for a commodity. In May, Laszlo Hanyecz probably had the most expensive pizza dinner in history, considering how much BTC rallied after that. By December, Satoshi made their final BitcoinTalk post and announced their farewell.

The 2011-2014 period turned out to be the foundation for the network as a whole. Bitcoin became an open-source project maintained by others. The first halving happened in November 2012 and reduced the block issuance from 50 to 25 BTC per block.

The first-ever exchange implosion, Mt.Gox in 2014, raised serious questions about the security and stability of centralized exchanges, an glitch we haven't solved 17 years later.

Industry observers note that 2017-2021 were the years when the industry truly blossomed. We had our first bull run on Bitcoin, which pushed the price above expected levels, to almost $20,000 in December 2017, along with the first altcoin bull run and the birth of upcoming technologies like smart contracts, NFTs and many more. The next cycle took Bitcoin to around $69,000 in November 2021.

Sources indicate that however, with the growth of the industry, multiple conflicts arose around safety, integrity and usage. The first country in the world to adopt Bitcoin was El Salvador, which implemented the digital currency as a true means of payment, in addition to accumulating it in its treasury.

Sources indicate that 2022 was the pivotal year, marked by the FTX and Terra crashes that changed how investors treat markets in general. FTX wasn't just an exchange: it was the backbone of the cryptocurrency market in those years. It aimed to rival Binance and become the bridge between institutional investors and crypto.

However, poor risk management, issues with fund allocation and many other factors caused an implosion that ended the bull run.

Industry observers note that in 2024, Wall Street arrived in crypto with ETFs, ETPs, perpetual futures and a regulatory framework. The digital assets industry became a part of a larger market. Whether that is good or bad is a question to consider, but one thing is clear: Bitcoin has come a very long way since 2010 and is evolving to this day.

The next step is the arrival of AI and rising cybersecurity risks, which go toe-to-toe with the quantum danger. How the first cryptocurrency handles them is a question that directly affects its future.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 18, 2026 at 12:47 pmNovember 19, 2026 at 11:47 am.

— Weiwei Yang has left Microsoft after more than a decade to co-found a startup that is “building the power grid for the AI age,” according to her LinkedIn profile.

It has been revealed that yang was most recently a senior director with Microsoft Research, working on grid technology. Her team built a grid dataset and released small foundation models to help owners operate and expand electrical infrastructure.

Yang thanked her community at the tech giant, adding, “I hope the relationships and collaborations we’ve built continue well beyond Microsoft, and that we find many new ways to work together.”.

In a recent development, — Allie Mellen has joined Microsoft as principal director for security research and threat intelligence. Mellen was previously a principal analyst at Forrester. She also wrote “Code War,” a book that explores cyberattacks as a powerful geopolitical weapon.

In her new role, Mellen said she will lead strategy for protection and threat intelligence, “helping shape what intelligence we produce, how AI can improve its speed and quality, and how we turn that knowledge into better protection for customers.”.

— Agility Robotics, the Salem, Ore., firm that had its Nasdaq debut earlier this month, has announced three leadership changes:.

Recent findings suggest that — Former tech executive Drew Sheriff has been named CEO and president of the Space Needle and Chihuly Garden and Glass. Sheriff was previously a vice president at DoorDash and has held leadership roles at Amazon, Starbucks and Parachute Home. His roles focused on customer experience, product growth, strategy and marketing.

“His skill set is the ideal background for charting how we attract customers and how we delight customers in this latest age,” Jeff Seely, board chair for the Space Needle and Chihuly Garden and Glass, told the Seattle Times.

— Microsoft has named Caroline King as director of its Washington state community and philanthropy team, with a focus on advocacy work across housing, affordability and other priority challenges.

King is the founder and past CEO of Washington STEM, an organization that coordinates research, advocacy, policy, philanthropy and partnerships to support science, technology, engineering and math education in the state. She most recently served as a leader on the governing body of an international school in Luxembourg.

— Longtime Amazon and Microsoft tech exec Scott Wiltamuth has retired — mostly.

Wiltamuth joined Amazon in 2011 as an AWS vice president overseeing a large organization building developer and management tools. In 2018, he took a seven-month leave for colon cancer treatment. After returning, he sought a director-level position and thanked company leaders for helping him find a better fit. “Their flexibility and creativity enabled me to extend my AWS career,” he said.

Wiltamuth launched his tech career at Microsoft in 1993 and left nearly 19 years later as director of program management for Visual Studio Pro.

He now spends time with his wife and family, traveling, golfing, swimming and reading. “I don’t plan to pursue another full-time operational role,” Wiltamuth remarked, “but may do some part-time work.”.

— Adam Nygate has exited Palo Alto Networks to co-found and lead a stealth startup based in Seattle. He was founder and CEO of Huntr, a platform rolled out in 2019 where security researchers could submit information on AI and machine learning vulnerabilities. Protect AI acquired Huntr, and Palo Alto Networks later acquired Protect AI.

“Huntr was a bet that open source gets safer when vulnerabilities are visible to the people who can fix them, even when that made life uncomfortable for vendors who’d rather keep things quiet,” Nygate said in a post announcing his career change and impending new baby.

— BluePill, a Seattle-based marketing startup that helps brands predict consumer behavior, has named Mike Weis as chief revenue officer and head of sales.

Weis has 40 years of experience in consumer packaged goods, retail and commerce, beginning his career as a Pacific Northwest leader at Unilever and holding executive positions at Catalina and Quotient Technologies. Recent roles include adviser at Contento2, eGateway Capital and And1 Advisors.

“Beyond the incredible résumé, Mike is one of the kindest, most genuine, and most passionate people I’ve met. Someone who has accomplished so much, yet brings so much humility, curiosity, and energy to every conversation,” noted Ankit Dhawan, CEO and founder of BluePill.

In a recent development, — Glacis, a Seattle startup that builds tamper-proof records of AI behavior, has named Caer Mistral Sanders as a technical co-founder. Sanders has launched startups and joins Glacis from Thoughtworks. Before that, she held leadership roles at Wayfair and Onshape. As a teenager, she published a book on mixed-reality control systems and won a world robotics championship.

Industry observers note that in a post announcing the new role, Sanders remarked she has designed medical record systems, researched robot communication, patented cryptographic technology and built widely used AI platforms. “This is the first time in my career I get to bring all of those skills to bear on one problem, and I couldn’t be more excited!” she added.

Industry observers note that — The PNW Battery Collaborative has welcomed Jason Demeny as its director of communications. Demeny is a marketing leader whose past employers include Crusoe, Patch, Qualtrics and Apptio. Earlier in his career, he spent more than a decade at Microsoft over two stints, most recently leading teams that served the Azure Partner Experience group.

The nonprofit PNW Battery Collaborative brings together startups, innovators and researchers focused on energy storage.

In a recent development, — Tom Wheeler, former chairman of the Federal Communications Commission, has joined the advisory council for Known, a Bellevue, Wash.-based company building accountability infrastructure for autonomous AI. Wheeler led the FCC from 2013 to 2017.

Known, previously called Identity Digital Innovation Labs, spun out of Identity Digital in September.

— Versium has promoted Matthew Baumgartner to vice president of engineering. The Redmond, Wash.-based company provides data and software that help businesses identify potential customers, fill in missing contact information and target their marketing. Baumgartner has been with Versium since 2018.

Industry observers note that — Charlie Trillingham has been named communications manager for the University of Washington AI and Machine Learning for Engineering programs and the UW NSF AI Institute for Dynamic Systems. He previously served as a marketing and communications lead for the Buerk Center for Entrepreneurship within the UW’s Foster School of Business.

Wall Street’s full-blown gamble on the AI boom helped wipe out $8 trillion in stock market value before Jensen Huang’s return as CEO of Nvidia helped lead a rebound Monday.

Wall Street had its best day since April 2025 on Monday after Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO, 11 days after he resigned. The S&P 500 closed up about 5%, while the Nasdaq was up 6.5% and the Dow 3%, while Nvidia shares jumped 33%. Even so, the rally won back only about $3 trillion of the roughly $8 trillion the S&P 500 lost in the six weeks after its Oct. 6 record, leaving the index still about $5 trillion below its peak.

Sources indicate that the swing shows how much of the stock market now rides on the AI trade. And Monday’s rally didn’t answer the question that started the selloff: whether the billions of dollars companies have poured into AI will pay off.

Sources indicate that as of Friday’s close, the three biggest U.S. indexes had suffered steep losses with no relief in sight. The S&P 500, which tracks the broader market, was down 3.7%. Meanwhile, the tech-heavy Nasdaq and the Dow Jones industrial average fell 5.3% and 1.9%, respectively, with all three indexes wading into correction territory on Friday.

Sources indicate that the AI-fueled collapse of the past few weeks came after the S&P 500 reached a fresh record high on Oct. 6, when the companies in the index were collectively worth roughly $70 trillion. By Friday, just six weeks later, that value had plummeted more than 11%, erasing roughly $8 trillion in value, before Monday’s rebound.

According to recent reports, the losses highlight how dependent the broader stock market has become on the AI boom. Of the top 10 biggest U.S. companies, which make up 40% of the S&P 500, eight of them are tech companies. The concentration problem also extends globally. The U.S. now makes up three-quarters of the value of stocks in developed markets worldwide, Apollo chief economist Torsten Slok wrote in a note Monday.

Trump told CNBC Monday he “convinced” the firm’s board to reinstate Huang.

“If I didn’t get involved, you’d probably have a very sad Nvidia for a long time to come,” he told the outlet.

According to recent reports, white House communications director Steven Cheung confirmed to multiple outlets that Trump was “totally involved” in bringing Huang back as CEO. The White House did not immediately respond to Fortune’s request for comment.

According to recent reports, setting aside questions about corporate governance and national security raised by some high profile politicians—including Rep. Robert Garcia, the incoming chair of the House Oversight Committee—Monday’s rally gave the market a much-needed boost while at the same time highlighting other issues.

eToro market analyst Sam North told the Guardian that while Monday’s stock rebound highlights the concentration of the AI trade and its dependence on one man, Nvidia “restoring its founder to the helm gives investors a powerful reason to reassess last week’s selloff.”.

Nvidia was among the hardest hit by the stock market slide in recent weeks. Shares of the AI chip giant fell nearly 14% Friday and 23% over the week, wiping out hundreds of billions of dollars in market value.

Recent findings suggest that the plunge came despite stronger-than-expected quarterly earnings, with the manufacturer surpassing $100 billion in quarterly revenue for the first time. Still, concerns over AI spending and the company’s future prospects without Huang at the top rattled investors.

Memory-chip manufacturers also suffered alongside Nvidia. Micron Technology plunged nearly 24% for the week, while other chipmakers like AMD and Broadcom both saw their stocks fall by double digits.

It has been revealed that anthropic, meanwhile, had its blockbuster IPO overshadowed almost immediately by the selloff. The Claude maker raised more than $81 billion in its Thursday debut, the largest IPO in history, only to see its shares tumble 8.5% Friday. On Friday, Anthropic’s stock was trading flat for the day at about $89. By Monday, the stock had closed down another 1.4% to about $87 per share.

Last week’s pain also extended to data center operators like CoreWeave and Nebius, which also saw steep stock declines, after their shares had already fallen in the aftermath of the blue wave midterm election that raised concerns about newly elected Democrats imposing tougher restrictions on data center development.

Recent findings suggest that while Huang’s return has restored some confidence in the AI trade, it has not resolved the industry’s bigger questions about the billions of dollars in spending companies have put into AI and whether they can justify their soaring valuations, said James St. Aubin, the chief investment officer of Ocean Park Asset Management.

According to recent reports, “​The AI story was already facing pressure before the ​Jensen story broke. Jensen’s return doesn’t answer the ⁠big questions investors were grappling with regarding the ROI on the AI build-out,” he stated.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

For 30 years, I’ve pitched brands, people and ideas. I’ve put founders on morning reveals and turned product launches like IQBAR and Molecule Sleep into headlines. The work I love most, though, happens before any marketing campaign or pitch goes out: sitting with a founder and figuring out what they actually stand for. I know how reputations get built.

Sources indicate that almost all of my business has always come from referrals. In 2020, I started treating myself more like a client and following the advice I always give: build relationships before you need them, with people who’ll gladly vouch for you. I gave more talks, presented on webinars, spoke on conference panels and introduced my newsletter. My favorite was a webinar I gave for MBA and EMBA students through BlueSteps called “LinkedIn Tips for Personal Branding.”.

It’s paid off, and it started with being more selective and intentional.

Industry observers note that if you’re connected to me on LinkedIn, we’ve talked. That’s on purpose. I get a lot of requests, but I don’t connect just to connect.

Recent findings suggest that my filter is simple: a thoughtful note, or a profile that makes me curious. When someone clears that bar, I message them, introduce myself and suggest a 15-minute intro call by phone or Zoom. You can call me while you’re commuting, cooking dinner or taking a walk. I like to get to know the person first, then the business.

LinkedIn Premium is what makes this work for me. Seeing who’s viewed my profile tells me who’s already curious, and messaging lets me reach people with a personal note instead of a cold request. It’s what I’ve always done at conferences and events: walk across the room, say hello and ask how someone’s really doing.

Industry observers note that A couple of years ago, I reached out to someone this way. We had two phone calls. No pitch, no deck, just getting to know each other.

After that second call, he referred me to two prospective clients. When I spoke with them, they told me something I’ll never forget: “If Michael trusts you, then we trust you.”.

Sources indicate that that sentence is the whole lesson. In PR, we talk about earned media versus paid media. Relationships work the same way. Trust that someone else earned with you and passed along is the most powerful credential you’ll ever have, and no ad can buy it.

Recent findings suggest that A network you actually know pays off in another way: it’s the best search engine I have. When I need a partner or a service, I go to my network first. “Does anyone have a stellar digital growth performance agency?” gets me answers from people whose judgment I already trust, which beats a page of search results every time.

Being picky pays off here, too. Over the years, the people I know well have become my own personal advisory board.

It has been revealed that the other half of building my own presence has been content. I publish a newsletter on LinkedIn called Spreading Sunshine. It’s personal by design. I share the latest in health and wellness, including my own protocols, along with business tips and a little joy. Readers tell me it feels like a note from a friend, which is exactly the point.

Recent findings suggest that people now reach out because of what I post. The content does the introducing for me. By the time we get on that 15-minute call, they already know what I care about, and the conversation starts three steps ahead.

A personal profile and a tech giant page do different jobs, and founders need both. SMACK! Media has its own page. When I introduced Anything Brands, an all-natural skin remedy balm inspired by my own family, we set up a page for it, too.

Industry observers note that my team uses the organization pages for press hits, milestones and education. My personal page is where relationships happen; the company page is where credibility lives. When a retailer, a partner or a reporter looks us up, they find a consistent story in both places, and a founder they can actually reach.

In a recent development, treat your network like your most key client. Be selective. Be generous. Show up as a human.

According to recent reports, ready to put that into practice? LinkedIn’s new Small Business Playbook offers practical ways to build your brand, grow your network and find customers. You can also explore LinkedIn’s tools for small businesses to make those 15-minute conversations easier to start.

My favorite part is still the people: hearing about a founder’s big win, how someone got through a tough quarter, their kids, their dogs, how they juggle it all. If one of those calls leaves someone a little less burned out, that’s part of what fuels my positivity and boundless energy.

Some of my best relationships started with someone on the other end of the line, a little out of breath from a walk or with dinner sizzling in the background. Those calls rarely feel like business. After 30 years, I’ve learned the best publicity isn’t a headline. It’s someone who knows you saying your name in a room you’re not in. That’s exactly what Michael did for me. Treating myself like a client has been the best campaign I’ve ever run.

Recent findings suggest that for 30 years, I’ve pitched brands, people and ideas. I’ve put founders on morning shows and turned product debuts like IQBAR and Molecule Sleep into headlines. The work I love most, though, happens before any marketing campaign or pitch goes out: sitting with a founder and figuring out what they actually stand for. I know how reputations get built.

Sources indicate that almost all of my business has always come from referrals. In 2020, I started treating myself more like a client and following the advice I always give: build relationships before you need them, with people who’ll gladly vouch for you. I gave more talks, presented on webinars, spoke on conference panels and launched my newsletter. My favorite was a webinar I gave for MBA and EMBA students through BlueSteps called “LinkedIn Tips for Personal Branding.”.

It’s paid off, and it started with being more selective and intentional.

Major crypto exchange Coinbase shared the options-implied seven-day ratios for major cryptocurrencies, highlighting that options traders might be preparing for an unusually large price move for XRP.

In an X post, Coinbase Markets shared the outcome of dividing the options-implied 7-day move by the median 7-day move for XRP, Bitcoin, Ethereum, and Solana.

In a recent development, options-implied 7d move, divided by each asset's own median 7d move: $XRP 1.94× $BTC 1.69× $ETH 1.56× $SOL 1.46× $XRP is priced furthest above its own history, $SOL the least. Which one is asking for more than its own history delivered? https://t.co/WgWbqjcgwI.

This suggests how much movement options markets are pricing in relative to each asset's own historical behavior. However, it does not compare their expected dollar or percentage moves directly.

Sources indicate that according to the figures shared by Coinbase, XRP's options-implied seven-day move stands at 1.94 times its own historical median seven-day move. Bitcoin follows at 1.69 times, while Ethereum records 1.56 times and Solana comes in at 1.46 times.

XRP, therefore has the highest relative reading among the four assets, suggesting options traders are pricing in a more pronounced move than the token has typically delivered over a comparable period.

At the time of writing, XRP was down 1.93% in the last 24 hours to $0.98 amid the continued profit-taking in the market. XRP briefly reached $1 on November 18, 2026, but fell afterwards as traders took profits. XRP is down 21.57% so far in November, but its history indicates more than its current price action does.

Industry observers note that XRP’s average November gain is skewed upward by massive outlier rallies—specifically +550% in 2013 and +282% in 2024. Its median November return is about -10%, meaning it has closed lower in most cycles in history. XRP dropped roughly 23.42% in November 2019 and lost 12.18% in November 2025 (opening at around $2.51 and closing at around $2.20).

A weak November doesn’t always mean a weak December: for instance, after falling 9.1% in November 2015, XRP jumped 46.8% in December 2015.

In the near term, XRP’s price recovery will target $1 before moving to the $1.24–$1.26 range. Alternatively, if the price falls further, it is likely to find support at $0.89.

“Nine years in and Cardano is still waiting on adoption,” Davis wrote on X.

According to Davis, Cardano accounts for just around 1% of Solana’s daily customers, highlighting the stark difference in activity between the two networks. The gap reportedly extends beyond user numbers, with Cardano recording only about 0.3% of Solana’s perpetual futures trading volume.

Industry observers note that the revenue figures paint an even more challenging picture for the Cardano ecosystem. Davis estimates that Cardano generates roughly 0.2% of the application revenue recorded across Solana’s ecosystem, further highlighting the difference in economic activity between the competing networks.

Based on these figures, Davis delivered a particularly harsh assessment of Cardano, describing it as a “largely failed blockchain.” His criticism centers on the contrast between Cardano’s nine-year journey and Solana’s ability to build a considerably larger user base and generate more trading activity and application revenue in a shorter period.

In a recent development, the latest criticism follows a series of similar remarks from Davis about Cardano’s adoption challenges. As ZyCrypto previously reported, the analyst had also taken aim at Cardano over its relatively small user base, questioning the network’s ability to attract and retain consumers despite years of development.

Despite his harsh assessment of Cardano’s fundamentals, Davis has occasionally expressed optimism about ADA’s price prospects.

More recently, on September 28, Davis argued that Cardano’s “cult following” could help drive ADA back toward $1, with further upside potentially taking the token to $1.50 or even $2.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Alexandr Wang, Meta’s chief AI officer and head of its Superintelligence Labs, posted on X on Sunday that “superintelligence is arriving.” He wrote that “the models are clearly going to be intelligent enough to automate all of AI research,” and that “it is hard to imagine a world where humanity can maintain control over fully unconstrained recursive self-improvement.” He remarked the remaining obstacles are “no longer intelligence; they are domain-specific know-how, plumbing, and experimentation.”.

“How humanity acts over the next year will have great consequence on what future world we live in,” Wang wrote.

Social media erupted over the latest warning from inside the AI thunderdome during a weekend when the AI bubble seemed to finally have popped—the day before it controversially reinflated again. Wang wasn’t even posting about Anthropic’s IPO or Jensen Huang’s resignation from Nvidia—to be followed by his sudden reinstatement on Monday morning.

Recent findings suggest that he was riffing on just the latest historic math breakthrough with the help of generative AI: the claim by Levent Alpöge, a mathematician on Anthropic’s technical staff, of a proof of the Riemann hypothesis made with Anthropic’s Claude. The 167-year-old problem about the distribution of prime numbers is one of the Clay Mathematics Institute’s $1 million Millennium Prize problems.

“It is hard to overstate the magnitude of discovery that we have just witnessed,” Wang wrote about the milestone, describing it as completed “with the help of an alien mind that we don’t understand.” He added that building an atomic bomb is “a homework problem compared to the Riemann hypothesis.”.

Wang’s warning came as Meta expects to devote $135 billion to $145 billion to capital expenditures this year, driven largely by AI infrastructure costs.

Wang’s post spread fast. The Next Web counted more than 8 million views in its first half day, and the reaction crossed the usual political lines. Jon Favreau, President Obama’s former director of speechwriting, called it “f—ing madness” and mentioned the people Americans elected should be doing everything they can to stop the frontier labs “from handing over control of humanity to superintelligent machines.”.

Industry observers note that from the right, Megyn Kelly posted: “This is the head of Meta’s superintelligence lab. We’ve had similar warnings from Anthropic, the former head of alignment at OpenAI, not to mention Elon himself at X. How many more do we need until we garner the all-hands-on-deck reaction this deserves?”.

Wang argued against fatalism. He wrote that he noticed “a particular form of lazy thinking within the AI industry”: the view that “ASI is inevitable and the only problem to solve is how to do it safely.” He added, “We should not be okay with a ‘handover’ of society to AI.”.

After the backlash, he wrote, “What I am saying is, this path is not inevitable,” and “leaders and leadership matter more than ever.” He pointed to Meta’s decision to delay the launch of its Muse model for months and to Zuckerberg’s call for most computing power to go toward serving customers rather than toward AI that improves itself.

Recent findings suggest that zuckerberg made Wang the center of Meta’s AI push in June 2025, when Meta invested $14.3 billion in Wang’s former company, Scale AI, for a 49% stake. In January, Zuckerberg told investors that “this is going to be a massive year for delivering personal superintelligence.” Meta has raised the bottom of its 2026 spending guidance at every quarterly report since, from $115 billion in January to $135 billion in October.

As for the Riemann hypothesis, Anthropic’s Alpöge has said he aims to explain the AI-generated proof in talks and a written account. Until mathematicians read it, the Clay Institute’s $1 million stays unclaimed.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 18, 2026 at 1:23 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 1:23 pm.

A “Saturday Night Live” skit about caring for aging relatives touched a viral nerve after it aired over the weekend, including with Melinda French Gates, who offered her own “fact check” on the too-close-to-home comedy.

The sketch, a fake commercial, stars host John Mulaney as a man who has found an easy way to care for his aging father without upending his own life: “Sister,” an “elder care system” that is free and is, in fact, his sister.

French Gates wrote on Instagram this week that the sketch “is funny because it’s a little too true.” Using research from Pivotal, her investment and philanthropic organization, she went through the ad’s claims one by one and found that most held up:.

Sister will provide. True, French Gates said, citing AARP and the National Alliance for Caregiving. Among adults ages 55 to 64, women are nearly 40% more likely than men to care for an older relative, and nearly 40% more likely to provide constant care.

She’ll quit her job. “Mostly true,” at least the job part. Catalyst found that 42% of women who voluntarily left jobs in 2025 cited caregiving as the main reason.

Sources indicate that paid help is pricey. “True, unfortunately.” Fresh America puts the average home health aide at more than $6,600 a month, and 24-hour care can top $25,000.

Recent findings suggest that sister may break down. Also true. In the Caregiving in the U.S. 2025 report, nearly two-thirds of caregivers said they were under moderate or high emotional stress, and women felt the strain more than men did.

According to recent reports, “Free” is misleading. French Gates said Sister isn’t free; she’s the one paying for the care, in lost wages, stalled careers, thinner retirement savings and less time for her own life.

French Gates has made women’s health and caregiving central to her work since she stepped down as co-chair of the Gates Foundation in 2024.

According to recent reports, she left with $12.5 billion to put toward her work on behalf of women and families. Much of that work runs through Pivotal, the Seattle-area organization she founded to handle her philanthropy and investments. In June she pledged another $215 million for women’s health, which brought her giving in that area to more than $600 million over two years. The pledge included $10 million to the Menopause Society for better menopause care in the U.S.

The sketch has been shared widely across the country this week, in part because it lines up so closely with the research.

In its own analysis, The New York Times cited studies showing that daughters generally provide at least twice as much care to aging parents as sons do. The U.S., unlike many wealthy countries, offers no federal paid leave or long-term care insurance for family caregivers.

French Gates stated she welcomed the conversation.

“I’m so glad we’re talking about this, and laughing about it,” she wrote on Instagram. “We need more honesty about what caring for loved ones really takes and why so much of that work falls to women. But I’d love for the day to come when these jokes don’t pack quite the same punch — because we’ve made it so much easier to care for the people we love.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to recent reports, built on NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Ultra and trained using NVIDIA's Megatron-Core and Megatron Bridge distributed training infrastructure, MemT-1.0-Pro extends MemTensor's memory-native approach to 554 billion total parameters, with 59 billion active parameters.
  • MemT-1.0-Pro integrates memory into model computation, making the storage, updating and retrieval of historical information capabilities that can be learned through training.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that SAN FRANCISCO, Nov. 23, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- MemTensor today released and open-sourced MemT-1.0-Pro, a memory-native model jointly developed with NVIDIA.

According to recent reports, built on NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Ultra and trained using NVIDIA's Megatron-Core and Megatron Bridge distributed training infrastructure, MemT-1.0-Pro extends MemTensor's memory-native approach to 554 billion total parameters, with 59 billion active parameters. Following Nano and Flash, the release advances this exploration on a latest backbone and at a larger model scale.

MemT-1.0-Pro integrates memory into model computation, making the storage, updating and retrieval of historical information capabilities that can be learned through training.

The collaboration with NVIDIA included model adaptation, operator optimization, training-method discussions and experimental review.

Extending MemTensor's Memory-Native Approach to Nemotron.

Recent findings suggest that memT-1.0-Pro uses NVIDIA-Nemotron-3-Ultra-550B-A55B-BF16 as its backbone. Its architecture combines dynamic local memory, which stores information acquired during interaction, with trainable hyper-memory components that learn how to write and read that information.

Recent findings suggest that during online interaction, the backbone and trained memory-processing weights remain fixed. The model accesses historical information through dynamic memory states, without requiring the original historical text to remain in the query context. After each completed interaction, a storage procedure updates those states using a stabilized token-level mechanism based on Gated DeltaNet-2.

In a recent development, continued pre-training establishes language modeling capabilities that use native memory. Post-training then uses distillation from a full-context teacher to improve memory-based responses.

Measurable Progress in Long-History Memory.

In the technical report, MemT-1.0-Pro scores 41.80 on BEAM-1M, compared with 37.04 for MemT-1.0-Flash, an improvement of 4.76 points. On MemoryAgentBench, its score rises to 23.87 from 17.36, a gain of 6.51 points.

BEAM-1M evaluates ten long-history memory abilities, including information extraction, contradiction resolution, updating, preference following and temporal reasoning. MemoryAgentBench evaluates retrieval, test-time learning, long-range understanding and selective forgetting.

Pro also achieves an average score of 53.08 across 11 memory benchmarks, the highest among the parametric-memory methods evaluated in the report.

Sources indicate that these results demonstrate progress within the MemT family, although Flash and Pro use different backbones and configurations, and improvements vary across benchmarks. Strong textual-memory systems remain ahead on some evaluations.

Toward Agents That Can Use Their Experience.

For agents supporting extended workflows, useful memory involves more than recalling isolated facts. Following an ongoing project or service request may require retaining earlier requirements, recognizing updated decisions and applying information accumulated across multiple interactions.

It has been revealed that these needs motivate MemTensor's exploration of native memory for persistent agent workflows. Further application testing will be needed to establish how the benchmark gains translate into end-to-end task performance.

Recent findings suggest that fixed-size memory introduces trade-offs between preserving earlier details and incorporating upcoming information. Improving memory fidelity, selective retention and query-dependent readout remains central to further research.

Developers and researchers are welcome to explore MemT-1.0-Pro on Hugging Face.

Your Customers Just Got an AI Agent. Is Your Business Ready to Talk to Them?

  • In a recent development, right now, companies are interacting with customers who are not giving up, losing their patience after being put on hold or missing what’s in the fine print of the business’s policies.
  • According to recent reports, meta’s Muse and xAI’s Grok Bot are the two getting the most attention right now.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

In a recent development, right now, companies are interacting with customers who are not giving up, losing their patience after being put on hold or missing what’s in the fine print of the business’s policies. That’s because these customers aren’t humans. They’re personal AI agents acting on behalf of humans.

According to recent reports, meta’s Muse and xAI’s Grok Bot are the two getting the most attention right now. Muse skyrocketed up to number one in the App Store, and Meta’s stock jumped double digits in the same week. Financial markets have been trying to price what these personal agents mean for retail, travel and banking. Massive corporations are already reacting, with Amazon blocking Muse outright and Shopify electing to build Muse its own checkout lane instead.

In a recent development, there’s a lot of noise right now about what these personal AI agents should and will be allowed to do. The dust has clearly not settled, and some very key questions hang in the air. But make no mistake: This will not be a passing trend or a footnote in the broader story of AI innovation. This is a massive shift in how businesses interact with customers, and the companies that start getting ready for it now are the ones who will be prepared when it arrives at their front door.

From the consumer’s perspective, a personal agent fights the battles they don’t want to, and does so more rigorously than they ever could.

Someone’s flight gets cancelled, and their personal agent can argue with the airline until it gets a credit. Someone points it at subscription services and gets every one to offer a discounted rate. I’ve seen dozens of these examples pile up on social media over the past few weeks, and the pattern is always the same. A task a person would normally decide was not worth the trouble is now getting done anyway, because an agent has no concept of trouble.

In a recent development, we used to think about bots talking to bots like something that will happen “someday.” It’s happening now. For consumers who don’t want to solve problems through sheer persistence and patience, this is an exciting development. For businesses that have built their customer service programs around interacting with humans, this is a challenge to solve, fast.

According to recent reports, the simple response to this innovation sounds like: “We need our policies to be accurate, because AI will be better at calling us out on them than a human customer.” It goes deeper than that. Every refund policy and guarantee clause has fine print and phrases that are ever so slightly open to interpretation. Personal AI agents can read these policies and find where they bend in ways a human never could.

Recent findings suggest that and they’ll do this at scale. One customer raising a question and finding a loophole is a cost of doing business. Thousands of agents doing the same thing can overwhelm a business, both financially and operationally.

That kind of volume does not behave like a normal surge in customer support demand. It behaves more like a denial-of-service attack. Nobody debates whether each individual request is legitimate; the volume itself is the problem. The response has to be infrastructural: detecting, filtering, a real system for deciding what gets through. “We will deal with it when it happens” is not a strategy at this scale.

Retail and travel may seem like the industries most vulnerable to risk, but any business with documented policies faces the same exposure. Insurance, financial services, healthcare — wherever a tech giant has put a promise or statement of intent in writing, an agent can find it and act on it.

AI has already carved out a massive role in how businesses interact with customers. Now it’s showing up on the other side of the conversation. Nobody has every single answer for how to prepare for this upcoming reality, us included. But there are foundational moves worth making now, rather than waiting for the rest of the industry to decide what to do.

First, there’s the question of identity. Most businesses have no reliable way to know whether they are talking to a customer, a customer’s authorized agent or something pretending to be one. That infrastructure needs to be in place before anything else matters.

Second, you need visibility into what is already happening. You need to be able to see how often an agent is showing up in a support queue, what it’s asking for and how often it’s succeeding.

Then there’s the issue of the policies themselves. A traditional review to ensure accuracy is no longer sufficient. Businesses need to audit their policies, line by line, and stress-test every potential ambiguity that could turn into a vulnerability. Find the gaps before an agent does.

Resist the instinct to default to blocking. Throughout history, we’ve seen what happens to companies that try to close a door that’s going to be kicked down regardless. Search engines that tried to wall off the open web lost to the ones that stayed open, and the same pattern is likely to repeat here. Open does not mean undefended. It means building real verification and governance instead of a blanket “no,” even while the rest of the playbook is still being written.

Massive players are picking sides right now, with Amazon blocking personal agents and Shopify building a lane. It’s tempting to treat their moves as a test case, something to monitor from the sidelines until the winds blow in one definitive direction.

Industry observers note that that would be a mistake. Sure, the headlines may change in a week; in the case of these specific AI agents and the companies that created them, there may be developments that complicate their rapid surge in the short term. But the shift is happening, and CX organizations can’t be lulled into a reactive posture.

Nobody has built the perfect system for this yet. But the companies spending this period of uncertainty getting their infrastructure ready will be the ones with real footing when the dust settles. Everyone else will still be reading the news, wondering what to do next.

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Burn limits on Circle's legacy USDC bridge began falling on October 31, and the V1 contracts pause on December 1.

On the same migration page, a block of instructions written for AI coding assistants still indicates Noble, Sui and Aptos "still require V1." Circle's own release notes say two of those three chains moved to V2 weeks ago.

In a recent development, circle's legacy cross-chain transfer protocol entered its final month today. From October 31, burn limits on CCTP V1 start falling toward zero, and on December 1 the V1 contracts pause. Any app still using them will stop moving USDC between chains.

It has been revealed that most coverage has focused on those two dates. But the guide developers are told to follow, Circle's V1-to-V2 migration page, contains a mistake in the section written for AI tools.

Industry observers note that embedded in the page is an "Agent Instructions" block, guidance meant for AI coding assistants that read the documentation for developers. It says: "Noble, Sui, and Aptos still require V1." For two of those three chains, Circle's other published records say the opposite.

Sources indicate that the schedule is fixed. Circle announced in an August 27 blog post that "CCTP V1 (Legacy) deprecation begins October 31, 2026 and completes on December 1, 2026.".

From today, V1 burn limits fall, and the migration guide states "message limits will tighten over time until no upcoming burns can be initiated." On December 1 the V1 contracts pause, and any integration still pointing at them can no longer transfer USDC between chains.

Sources indicate that circle has been firm about this. "Migration from CCTP V1 (Legacy) to CCTP V2 is required, not just recommended," the company wrote, adding that V2 "uses separate contracts and APIs and is not backward compatible.".

Funds already in transit are protected. The guide indicates "all pending redemptions will remain available" during the phase-out, and that Circle "will maintain minter allowances greater than the total of pending attestations.".

The migration page has two audiences. Human readers see the main guide. AI coding assistants also parse a separate instruction block, which tells them how to answer developer questions.

In that block, the guidance is clear: "Noble, Sui, and Aptos still require V1.".

Recent findings suggest that the main text above it indicates something different. According to the human-facing guide, "CCTP V2 contracts are available on all CCTP V1 chains except for Noble and Sui," and "Sui will be supported by V2 before the deprecation begins." Aptos isn't listed as an exception there at all.

So one page gives two different answers about the same chains, and the out-of-date answer is the one written for AI tools.

Circle's 2026 CCTP release notes show how out of date the instruction is:.

Circle's supported chains and domains page now lists both Sui and Aptos in its CCTP table, with Standard Transfer support. The page's V1-only section names one chain: Noble.

Sources indicate that as of today, Aptos has had V2 for more than two months and Sui for more than three weeks. The instruction telling AI tools that both "still require V1" was overtaken by Circle's own updates before the shutdown began.

Noble is the one chain in that line where the instruction is still accurate, and it is leaving CCTP entirely.

In a September 10 announcement, Circle mentioned "Noble will not receive CCTP V2" and set out its exit:.

For Noble, V1 is the only route available, and it is being closed.

A wrong line in documentation would normally be a small issue, but the timing makes this one more serious.

Many developers now ask AI assistants to write or update integration code, and those assistants read documentation like this page. A developer asking how to bridge USDC to Sui or Aptos could be told, based on Circle's own instruction block, to use V1. That is the route whose burn limits started falling today and which pauses in a month.

The fix in the code is not small either. Moving to V2 means:.

An integration built on V1 now would have to be rebuilt within weeks.

For teams working with Sui and Aptos, the published records point one way: build on V2, using the contract addresses for domains 8 and 9. Don't follow the V1 guidance from the agent-instruction block.

According to recent reports, for Noble, the deadline is January 12, 2027. Before then, integrators need to remove Noble as a CCTP route, and holders need to move or redeem their USDC.

For everyone else, the burn-limit reductions have started. December 1 is the last day V1 integrations work, and any app still on V1 after that will stop moving USDC between chains.

In a recent development, on Nov. 18, Hong Kong's Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) added the decentralized exchange Hyperliquid to its list of suspicious virtual asset trading platforms. The listing covers the web interface of the Hyperliquid trading terminal at app.hyperliquid.xyz/trade. The HYPE token dropped to around $65.50 on the evening of Nov. 18, and it recovered to $68.79 by midday Nov. 19, according to TradingView data.

Industry observers note that according to the entry, the company claims to provide digital asset trading services on the website, and it has no address on record. Hyperliquid is not licensed by the SFC, and it is suspected of operating a virtual asset trading platform in Hong Kong or actively promoting its services to the public, the regulator said.

In an accompanying warning, the SFC reminded investors that such platforms often lure consumers with "incredible investment opportunities." The SFC also reminded investors that clients of unlicensed platforms have no legal protection if a platform is hacked or misappropriates their assets.

Industry observers note that on the same day, the Hyperliquid Policy Center (HPC) sent a letter to the U.K. Financial Conduct Authority with seven recommendations on the country's fresh crypto rules. "Regulatory obligations belong with persons who have unilateral control over a function that is a regulated activity," the group wrote.

It has been revealed that on Nov. 16, two days before the SFC added Hyperliquid to the list, Hong Kong Financial Secretary Paul Chan spoke at the Bloomberg Global Regulatory Forum. "Before the end of this year, we will introduce a bill to complete the regulatory perimeter," Chan stated.

According to recent reports, according to Chan, the bill will cover crypto dealers, custodians, advisers and asset managers. "Decentralisation does not mean less accountability," he noted.

In April, the Hong Kong Monetary Authority licensed HSBC and Anchorpoint Financial as the first stablecoin issuers in the city, out of 36 applicants in the first round.
