💡 Key Takeaways
  • Anthropic’s 5,300 employees are starting a latest week with more money than they could fathom just days ago.
  • The firm’s IPO sent its collective employee wealth soaring, putting the average non-founder staff’s estimated fortune at more than $44 million.
  • That means Anthropic has more centimillionaires among its ranks than there are living in the entirety of London, Paris, or Los Angeles.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Anthropic’s 5,300 employees are starting a latest week with more money than they could fathom just days ago.

The firm’s IPO sent its collective employee wealth soaring, putting the average non-founder staff’s estimated fortune at more than $44 million. But for 598 non-founder employees, they now have at least $100 million to their name, according to a report by private-markets investing firm Hill, cited by Reuters.

That means Anthropic has more centimillionaires among its ranks than there are living in the entirety of London, Paris, or Los Angeles. The only cities with more are San Francisco and New York City, according to wealth migration firm Henley & Partners.

Industry observers note that those estimates are based on Anthropic’s $83-per-share IPO price, a level the stock has yet to fall below. By Thursday’s close, shares had climbed to $97.17, putting the collective estimated wealth of Anthropic’s employees and seven cofounders at roughly $433 billion—more wealth than the entire bottom one-third of Americans, according to a viral analysis by Steve Rattner.

While Anthropic shares have since pulled back to around $88—making the total Anthropic staff equity closer to $350 billion—the wealth gains remain substantial.

Anthropic’s rise after being founded in 2021 has been meteoric. But critics have warned that the wealth generated by its rapid growth is also raising questions about who stands to benefit from the AI boom—and who could be left behind.

Former Chicago Mayor Rahm Emanuel, who appeared at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum earlier this month, stated changes need to be made to the tax code so that so much wealth cannot be preserved among a few people.

Recent findings suggest that “AI has the potential to create enormous prosperity. But if all that wealth flows to a handful of people at the top while working families struggle to get ahead, we’re not building an economy of the future,” he posted on X. “We’re repeating the mistakes of the past.”.

Hana Ivanhoe, senior manager of private sector campaigns and advocacy at anti-poverty nonprofit Oxfam America, echoed to Fortune that Anthropic’s IPO offers a striking example of how the AI boom could deepen existing economic divides.

“The level of wealth concentration that Anthropic’s IPO has precipitated is obviously jarring, and it’s emblematic of the extreme inequality that already characterizes our economy and is sure to be exacerbated by future IPOs like this one,” she stated.

That wealth is being generated amid growing questions about AI’s breakneck pace of development and its potential consequences for the job market—and even humanity itself.

It has been revealed that “It’s not only a problem that these IPOs are making a rich few even richer, it’s that they are getting richer at the expense of everyone else,” Ivanhoe added. “There’s both wealth inequality and inequality of impact at play here.”.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei’s net worth skyrocketed to some $21 billion with the IPO, but he has also voiced concerns about the consequences of AI driving that wealth.

“The thing to worry about is a level of wealth concentration that will break society,” he wrote in a letter released in January.

In response, Amodei, alongside his fellow six founders, committed to donate 80% of their Anthropic equity to philanthropy—and urged others to be more generous with their giving.

And while Amodei has also called for the AI industry to slow down development amid his own concerns about AI systems going rogue, being used in cyberattacks and bioterrorism, or causing serious economic disruption, Anthropic went through with its IPO, in part, because of a need for more financing to develop AI safely. Competitor OpenAI delayed its IPO until 2027.

Google acquires Seattle startup Howie and its AI scheduling assistant

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 18, 2026 at 2:03 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 2:03 pm.
  • Google is bringing Seattle-based Howie, maker of an AI scheduling assistant that works from your inbox, into its Google Labs division.
  • Sources indicate that terms of the deal were not disclosed this week.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 18, 2026 at 2:03 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 2:03 pm.

Google is bringing Seattle-based Howie, maker of an AI scheduling assistant that works from your inbox, into its Google Labs division.

Sources indicate that terms of the deal were not disclosed this week. Google Labs, the tech giant’s experimental arm, declared the acquisition in a post on X, saying it “can’t wait to learn from them as we build the next generation of intuitive AI tools together for small businesses.”.

Howie CEO and co-founder Austin Petersmith said on LinkedIn that the team will continue building Howie at Google. “Howie has always been built on top of Gmail and Google Calendar, so Google Labs is the perfect place for us to take this product to the next level,” he wrote.

It has been revealed that petersmith co-founded Howie around 2023 with CTO Dave Newman. The two first worked together in 2013 at Assembly, which Newman co-founded, and prototyped an AI assistant in 2015 before deciding the market wasn’t ready.

Sources indicate that we’re excited to welcome Howie to Google Labs! The @Howie_ai team has spent years figuring out scheduling and calendar management. We can’t wait to learn from them as we build the next generation of intuitive AI tools together for small businesses 🤝 https://t.co/8bzjebeGdD.

Users cc Howie on an email thread, and it coordinates meeting times, adds events to calendars, follows up as needed and flags scheduling conflicts. Customers set their own rules in an open-ended preferences document, such as “if it’s a pitch call, set it to 25 minutes and use Zoom.”.

Behind the scenes, Howie ran tasks through fine-tuned language models and looped in human scheduling experts when the AI wasn’t confident.

Howie raised a $6 million seed round led by True Ventures in September 2025, when it released publicly out of private beta. At the time, it had more than 1,000 paying customers, including startup founders, venture capitalists, recruiters, consultants and journalists, and was scheduling more than 5,000 meetings a week.

In a recent development, the deal comes as Google and rivals including OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta race to build AI agents that complete tasks on behalf of users. Google Labs acquired music generation platform ProducerAI earlier this year.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • What is WISEcode?Basically, we’re trying to solve what I call the food information crisis.
  • It has been revealed that this isn’t the first company you’ve started or been a big part of.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that if you’re like me, your approach to nutrition mostly involves squinting at a label, not recognizing any of the ingredients, and eating the thing anyway. Peter Castleman decided that wasn’t good enough. After four decades as an investor, including as Chairman and Managing Partner of J.H. Whitney & Co., where he played a role in investments tied to The North Face, Igloo and Herbalife, Peter came out of retirement to become the founder and CEO of WISEcode, an AI-powered food transparency platform that has mapped more than 840,000 products. He’s 70 years old and claims he’s never felt more excited about an idea, proving it’s never too late to chase a substantial idea.

Give us the elevator pitch. What is WISEcode?Basically, we’re trying to solve what I call the food information crisis. We literally don’t know two things: what’s in our food and what it does to us. At WISEcode, we’ve been spending a dozen years or so solving that. We’ve created what we call the Food Genome Project, which is really mapping the entire food system. So we now know exactly what’s in our foods, and we can tell you what it does for you. And that applies to consumers, policymakers, government people, industries, retailers, scientists, everyone. That information didn’t exist, and now it does.

It has been revealed that this isn’t the first company you’ve started or been a big part of. Why did you want to become a founder again?Well, I’m 70, okay? When I turned 50, I retired from my firm. I’m healthy. I eat generally well. But when you turn 50, you enter the kill zone for chronic disease, and chronic disease is 90% of our health problems, and 80% of chronic disease is driven by what we choose to do. We actually control most of our health outcomes. So I basically wanted to simply hack what I’m going to eat. I didn’t want to get cognitive issues. I didn’t want to get any late-onset chronic disease. But that hack doesn’t exist. It shocked me. It just doesn’t exist. So this passion became the business purpose of WISEcode, and I stated, “Okay, I’m gonna get this information. I’m going to do for me, I’m going to do for every single individual. I’m going to give them Food Truth.” Formally, I’ve probably been doing this for about 12, 13 years. Informally, I’ve been thinking about it for 20 years.

It has been revealed that when a business is a personal passion, do you have a process for figuring out whether it will be a passion for other people, too? Or do you just follow your heart?Like many people, I suffer from that latter part, which is letting your emotions get too far into stuff. I’ve always said, “Fall in love with your family and your friends, not your businesses.” It’s hard to do, because you develop passions. I have three tests I generally apply to any kind of activity. The first I call the North Star test: is it very clear that what you’re trying to do resonates with others? Is it going to be an aha moment or a so-what moment to the world? Number two, I call the sandbox test. How massive is your sandbox? How big is your addressable market? And how crowded is your sandbox? And then the third one I call the moat test, which is: can you build defensible business assets that prevent people from copying what you do? People will copy you in a second if you’re successful. If I’m not slam-dunk strong on all three tests, I try to stay away. I apply that to WISEcode. I apply it to everything I do. I’m better at it now than I was at 25.

How do you figure out if other people are interested in your idea when you don’t have a major budget?Social media and everything we have today are double-edged swords. But I use SurveyMonkey all the time. You can ask a question and, for not very much money, you can get 500, 1,000 really clear answers that help you evolve. You can do the same thing on social media tools. The tools out there today are so great. It used to be you’d have to hire McKinsey or Bain for a gazillion dollars, and they’d do a six-month study. Now, in a day, you can get better information than they ever gave you.

Recent findings suggest that what do you say to someone in their 50s who thinks, “I always wanted to do my own thing, but it’s too late”?First and foremost, I think you gotta be honest with yourself. Who are you? What do you love doing, and are you good at this? Late in your career, any time, if you don’t have the energy, the drive and the staying power, don’t do it. Because building companies is hard. You’re going to get knocked on your fanny a ton of times. You gotta get back up. You gotta inspire others around you. You gotta keep going when everyone indicates, “Don’t do it.” You’re gonna run out of money. You’re gonna have your spouse saying, “What the hell are you doing?” But if it’s in your DNA, it’s the greatest thing in the world. Most of my contemporaries are reducing their handicap on the golf course, and I’m spending 10 hours a day, seven days a week on WISEcode, and I love it. I wouldn’t change it for the world, but that’s me. The greatest joy I get, besides my love of my friends and family, is building businesses that actually make a difference, and if that’s in your DNA, do it. I think the only failure in life is not trying.

Zeno Power makes progress on an underwater power system that will eventually go nuclear

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Alan Boyle on Nov 19, 2026 at 7:00 amNovember 19, 2026 at 8:01 am.
  • Zeno Power has hit a major milestone in its push to build nuclear batteries for underwater use.
  • Sources indicate that the startup stated today that it successfully demonstrated an electrically heated Stirling generator in a controlled maritime setting in Washington state.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Alan Boyle on Nov 19, 2026 at 7:00 amNovember 19, 2026 at 8:01 am.

Zeno Power has hit a major milestone in its push to build nuclear batteries for underwater use.

Sources indicate that the startup stated today that it successfully demonstrated an electrically heated Stirling generator in a controlled maritime setting in Washington state. The two-week demonstration produced electrical power outputs in excess of 20 watts, said Lindsey Boles, Zeno’s chief product officer.

“It’s a really big step for us — just solidifying our expertise in how to design these, and then confirming our ability to translate that into operational hardware that meets or exceeds what our customers need,” Boles told GeekWire.

According to recent reports, zeno is developing the power system with support from the Department of Defense as a follow-up to an initial $7.5 million contract awarded in 2023. The generator uses a Stirling engine to convert heat into electricity by cycling gas through heating and cooling phases in a closed cylinder.

Sources indicate that for the recent demonstration, the prototype device relied on an electric heating element. Future devices will instead rely on heat generated by the radioactive decay of strontium-90, a radioisotope that can be extracted from spent nuclear fuel.

It has been revealed that nuclear batteries have been in use for decades, primarily for space missions ranging from the Apollo moon shots to NASA’s Voyager spacecraft and Mars rovers. But the batteries being developed by Zeno Power promise to be at least four times more efficient than traditional radioisotope thermoelectric generators, Boles mentioned.

Sources indicate that boles stated the non-radiological test exceeded expectations. “There’s a difference between a design that works on paper and hardware that works in the field,” she said in a news release. “This is the moment our team has been building toward: proof that this technology works outside the lab.”.

In a recent development, long-lasting nuclear batteries could be used to power undersea sensor networks or recharge autonomous underwater vehicles. “There are a lot of applications, especially on the maritime front, that we really want electricity for,” Boles noted. “And we really don’t need a ton of it. But we need it to be really reliable, and we need it to be long endurance, and we need it to be self-managed. … I think of it like a slow Tesla supercharger on the seabed.”.

Retired Navy Adm. John Richardson, former chief of naval operations and a member of Zeno’s board of directors, called the recent test an “important step toward undersea superiority.”.

Sources indicate that “Protecting maritime infrastructure and powering distributed systems at sea requires energy; energy that lasts for years, not days or months,” Richardson said in a written statement. “As competition intensifies in contested domains, powered subsea systems will help keep us ahead. Zeno Power has steadily reduced risk, proven its technology, built a supply chain, and prepared to scale production.”.

In a recent development, next year, Zeno Power looks to install a radioisotope heat source in its generator and test the system in a water tank under controlled laboratory conditions. If those tests are successful, Zeno will move forward with the first operational seabed deployment of its radioisotope-fueled maritime system later in 2027.

Sources indicate that the maritime battery isn’t Zeno’s only product. The company is also working on a nuclear-powered heater system for spacecraft, with a demonstration on the lunar surface planned as early as 2028. Zeno’s broader vision is to provide long-lasting, reliable power on the moon and Mars, and in extreme environments on Earth.

Since its founding in 2018, Zeno has secured $105 million in private capital and has brought in $60 million in contracts with the Pentagon and NASA. The company has more than 95 employees at locations in Seattle, California and Washington, D.C., with the largest contingent working at its engineering headquarters in Seattle’s South Lake Union district.

Industry observers note that binance will delist five crypto spot trading pairs within the next 24 hours on Nov. 20, 2026, following a review.

To protect its customers and to ensure a high-quality trading market, Binance conducts regular reviews of all listed spot trading pairs; it may delist certain spot trading pairs for various reasons, including low liquidity and trading volume.

Binance will delist GAS/TRY, HBAR/BNB, HIVE/TRY, KSM/TRY and ZAMA/TRY pairs on November 20, 2026 at 03:00 UTC, according to an official announcement published on November 18.

Sources indicate that four of the five affected pairs are related to the Turkish lira (TRY), while the last one is HBAR/BNB. The decision affects trading between these specific assets and does not mean the cryptocurrencies themselves are being completely delisted from Binance.

The exchange clarified that users will still be able to trade the affected tokens through other available spot trading pairs on its platform.

Recent findings suggest that binance will terminate Spot Trading Bots services for the spot trading pairs simultaneously where applicable. Users are strongly advised to revision and/or cancel their Spot Trading Bots prior to the cessation of services for Spot Trading Bots to avoid any potential losses.

Sources indicate that in related news, Binance Margin will initiate a routine cleanup of Cross Margin accounts with collateral valued at less than 1 USD (or equivalent in other assets), effective from November 30, 2026 at 00:00 (UTC). The cleanup will be executed on a daily basis as an ongoing operational process.

Affected accounts include Cross Margin Accounts with a collateral value of less than 1 USD equivalent across all assets and no outstanding liabilities, as well as Margin Accounts with no capital activity in the past 6 months. Capital activity refers to any action that generates a capital flow.

For each eligible Small-Asset Account, the system will automatically transfer the collateral in users’ Margin Accounts to their Spot Accounts while the Margin Account functions remain normal, allowing users to transfer, borrow, or trade at any time after the cleanup.

Accounts with collateral equal to or exceeding 1 USD equivalent are not affected by this cleanup.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When Lang Walker, the late Australian billionaire property developer and philanthropist, and his wife, Sue Walker, first saw Yaukuve Levu Island, Kadavu, Fiji, surrounded by the Great Astrolabe Reef, the land was largely overgrown, with the remains of a development that had never been completed.

“We anchored the boat out the front, looked at it and thought what a wonderful place this could be,” Sue Walker recalls. “It took eight years and an enormous amount of hard work to bring that vision to life.”.

That effort led to Kokomo Private Island, which officially opened in March 2017.

Today, the property features 21 beachfront villas and five hilltop residences, each with a private pool; three principal dining venues, with more than 80% of herbs and greens sourced from the island’s 5.5-acre organic farm; the Yaukuve Spa Sanctuary with its dedicated fitness center; and no shortage of adventure and cultural activities available to its guests.

It has been revealed that my husband and I had a chance to experience the tropical island paradise for ourselves in September. Throughout our stay, we were struck by Kokomo’s sheer natural beauty and how much the luxury hospitality experience was rooted in a genuine sense of place.

Sources indicate that increasingly, hotels and resorts highlighting local character rise to the top of travelers’ wishlists. Nearly three-quarters of luxury travelers won’t pay for accommodations that feel generic, per a report from Preferred Hotels & Resorts, and 77% of travelers prioritize authentic experiences representative of local culture, according to research from Booking.com.

Kokomo serves as a lesson in hospitality excellence — what it takes to succeed in a travel landscape increasingly defined by a desire for authenticity and local character. Here’s how every business can do the same.

According to recent reports, after a long day (or more) of travel, first impressions are key. Guests want to feel at ease and an immediate sense of place. But, sometimes, that’s the straightforward part. Sustaining that genuine warm welcome throughout the stay also matters.

Staff members at Kokomo give it its personality and make guests feel at home, often forming relationships that bring people back year after year, Walker says.

Additionally, Kokomo has developed a close relationship with the local community, where some staff members are from: supporting local employment, working with neighboring villages, and contributing to education, healthcare and community initiatives.

Industry observers note that “Authenticity comes from allowing those relationships and traditions to exist naturally, rather than trying to manufacture an experience for guests,” Walker states. “When someone shares a story about their village, introduces a guest to a local custom or folklore or even simply welcomes them with genuine Fijian hospitality, that’s what stays with people.”.

Recent findings suggest that our arrival and journey to Kokomo was seamless from the first “bula” (Fijian for “hello” and a wish for life and good health). After a 45-minute seaplane ride, we touched down on the crystalline blue waters in front of Kokomo. We were given a salusalu, a traditional garland worn around the neck, and coconut water, and listened to a group of staff members sing traditional Fijian welcome songs.

In a recent development, that warmth and hospitality extended throughout our time at Kokomo, across the interactions we had with staff and when we visited the nearby Dravuni Village, which is home to a small indigenous Fijian community. We heard traditional songs, learned about their hand-woven crafts, participated in a kava ceremony and toured the village with a staff member who’d grown up there.

The business lesson is this: Lean into what makes a destination special, and the cultural touchstones that define it, for an authentic welcome that extends from the first moment to the last.

Sources indicate that of course, as much as people want to soak up all a destination has to offer, they’ll spend a good portion of their vacation in their accommodations. Ideally, those accommodations capture the destination’s unique characteristics while prioritizing comfort.

From the beginning, the Walkers wanted Kokomo to feel like home, “albeit a rather extraordinary one,” where families could create lifelong memories with the privacy, space and luxury afforded by their own quiet corner of the island.

Recent findings suggest that “For me, true luxury isn’t about formality,” Walker notes. “It’s about comfort, freedom, being able to enjoy yourself without feeling constrained by the usual expectations of a hotel. Children should be able to run around, explore and have adventures, while their parents and grandparents can relax and enjoy the island in their own way.”.

According to recent reports, our one-bedroom beachfront villa, just steps from the ocean, felt sprung from the tropical landscape itself. The high ceilings, neutral stone and wood, and ample windows, the better to display the expansive patio with its private pool and the dazzling ocean view, created an indoor-outdoor flow with understated natural elegance.

When it comes to architecture, interior design, or landscape, embracing what sets the place surrounding it apart from any other, rather than competing with it, helps establish that seamless, one-of-kind experience guests won’t forget.

Whether a guest is a serious gourmet or not, meals will stand out as part of the experience (a three-times-a-day touchpoint). For remote resorts where guests rely solely on the dining on-site, it’s even more critical to deliver elevated, locally-defined experiences.

Early on, the Walkers realized they had access to the best ingredients on their doorstep — fresh seafood and the climate and space to grow much of the island’s own produce — and built their culinary philosophy around that, Walker notes.

“A fish caught locally that morning, vegetables picked from the garden, herbs cut just before they’re used,” she explains. “You can’t get much fresher than that. Building and operating a resort in such a remote location comes with enormous logistical challenges, so growing more of our own food and reducing our reliance on imported produce makes sense on many levels.”.

In a recent development, we had a chance to go on a tour with Kokomo’s executive chef Marty Kindleysides. He gave us an inside look at the island’s farm and hydroponic gardens, which help shape the menus across its restaurants: the Beach Shack on Kokomo’s western beach; Walker D’Plank, featuring Asian-influenced cuisine, near the arrival jetty; and the poolside Kokocabana, highlighting Italian-inspired dishes.

From the beautiful lunch Kindleysides prepared for us with farm-fresh ingredients like squash and kale, to all of the meals we enjoyed at the other dining venues, including a showstopping dinner by Chef Caroline during a curry-themed night at Walker D’Plank, the food was flavorful, intentional and reinforced a singular dining experience.

Guests should never feel like the food where they’re staying is an afterthought; it’s another opportunity — and a very memorable one — to showcase innovation and what makes a setting unique.

At a remote tropical resort like Kokomo, guests have the luxury of a picture-perfect natural setting offering once-in-a-lifetime activities. But striking the balance between making the most of the environment and protecting it is also critical.

Sources indicate that lang was an avid diver for most of his life and immediately recognized the wonder of the Great Astrolabe Reef. The Walkers saw it as their responsibility to look after it, so they set out to help guests experience and understand it.

“There’s something quite powerful about a child helping to plant coral, or a family learning about the individual manta rays that return to our waterways each season,” Walker says. “Suddenly conservation becomes personal. You’re no longer looking at a beautiful reef, rather, you’re beginning to understand how it works and why protecting it matters.”.

Sources indicate that we had the opportunity to meet with a marine biologist to learn about the manta rays and conservation efforts. Kokomo has partnered with Manta Project Fiji to research and protect Fiji’s reef manta rays since 2017. More than 500 manta ray sightings were recorded during the most recent monitoring period. We even went to look for them by boat, but unfortunately with it being the tail end of the season, didn’t spot any.

In a recent development, additionally, the marine biologist led us on a guided coral restoration tour, where we snorkeled over some of the current projects underway. More than 2,000 corals have been transplanted as part of Kokomo’s coral restoration. The island also has six active coral nurseries, which can support more than 10,000 corals per season.

Bringing guests into the very projects that protect the place they’re staying gives them destination-driven, extraordinary experiences while safeguarding them for future generations.

Relaxation means different things to different people, but centralizing spa and wellness options in one place, and melding personalized comfort with distinct ambiance, gives everyone the option to design an ideal routine to reset.

The Walkers wanted to build on the feeling guests have upon arrival — everyday life demands removed by the grandeur of nature — and developed the Yaukuve Spa Sanctuary with that in mind.

Recent findings suggest that “The gardens, the tropical landscape, the sense of privacy all contribute to the experience,” Walker notes. “I wanted guests to feel that they could completely switch off, even if only for an hour or two. I don’t think wellness needs to be complicated or overly prescriptive. Sometimes the greatest luxury is having the time and space to do what makes you feel good, without the schedule or expectation.”.

Industry observers note that we enjoyed Kokomo’s signature “Pacific Mastery Massage,” which incorporates centuries-old methods from traditional Fijian Bobo, combining variable pressure and rhythmic movement with the preferred oil blend. Before and after the service, we sipped iced hibiscus tea (the flower is often seen in Fijian landscaping) in the garden setting.

Industry observers note that guests will remember how a vacation makes them feel, so making sure they have the option to truly unwind, whatever that looks like for them, is key. Infusing it with a local twist means they won’t forget exactly where they experienced it.

At the end of the stay, as we departed on the one-hour helicopter ride back to the hangar, spotting our villa on the lush island encircled by a shock of turquoise, we came away already nostalgic for the trip, and with a deeper appreciation for Fiji’s natural beauty and vibrant culture.

We would love to return some day (maybe to snorkel with the mantas) — and that’s exactly what the Walkers intended.

In a recent development, “More than anything, I hope guests leave Kokomo feeling they’ve been part of something special,” Walker notes. “That they’ve spent quality time with the people they love, experienced the generosity of our Fijian team and discovered a part of the world they’ll always remember. If they leave feeling as though Kokomo is their island home, then we’ve achieved what we set out to do.”.

That effort led to Kokomo Private Island, which officially opened in March 2017.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy led to his ouster from Nvidia.
  • According to recent reports, within hours of Huang’s original (and ignominious) exit from Nvidia earlier this month, a “Stand With Jensen” petition circulated online, demanding Huang’s return to the manufacturer he’d cofounded in 1993.
  • Travis Kalanick, Uber’s pugnacious cofounder and former CEO, was both a signatory and especially vocal in his support.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy led to his ouster from Nvidia. Eleven days later, he’s back—the outcome Silicon Valley founders, watchers, and luminaries wanted all along.

According to recent reports, within hours of Huang’s original (and ignominious) exit from Nvidia earlier this month, a “Stand With Jensen” petition circulated online, demanding Huang’s return to the manufacturer he’d cofounded in 1993. Signatories included Elon Musk, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, Shopify CEO Tobias Lütke, Atreides Management CIO Gavin Baker, and Databricks CEO Ali Ghodsi, who wrote in the comments, “Nvidia runs on Jensen! Bring him back!”.

Travis Kalanick, Uber’s pugnacious cofounder and former CEO, was both a signatory and especially vocal in his support.

In a recent development, “Jensen is one of the great builders of our time,” Kalanick—himself ousted in 2017 from Uber amid compounding scandals—wrote in a public post on the “Stand With Jensen” site. “Liberty and civilizational progress depend on Jensen,” Kalanick declared. “He has erred, yes—to err is to be human—but I do not believe anything he has done rises to the bar of separating him from his organization. Jensen deserves fairness in adjudication and we must presume innocence until that adjudication proves otherwise beyond a reasonable doubt.”.

Huang’s return is a Rorschach test of sorts. Some critics see a corporate governance nightmare, while much of the wider public has memed or expressed horror at the circumstances of Huang’s initial resignation (widely described as potentially raising national security concerns). In Silicon Valley though, Huang’s ouster was an injustice that trumped any other aspects of the story. To tech, Huang remains the most indispensable of founders, a nearly godlike figure in a culture that worships “founder mode.”.

In a recent development, so, Huang’s return, however questionable it may be, is cause for celebration. Even the very circumspect Sam Altman, who’d previously expressed cautious sympathy for Huang (and who of course, went through a very similar ordeal), tweeted on X on Monday, “Jensen!” Musk, meanwhile, tweeted: “The mistake has been corrected.” Sarah Guo, the plugged-in founder of Conviction VC, welcomed Huang back. The chorus from tech was, in its way, relatively unanimous about just how positive this news was. (The markets agreed vigorously; Nvidia closed today up about 31%, after last week’s massive tech rout.) Meanwhile, for Nvidia’s board, it’s a dicey U-turn.

“Six days after Nvidia’s board remarked it had no intention of reinstating Jensen Huang as CEO, he’s back—before the board’s own independent investigation has reported anything, before he answers questions from Congress next week, and with no conditions attached (or at least none that anyone outside the boardroom can see),” said Nicole Bestard, founder of communications firm Quarter Horse Strategies, via email. “From a reputation standpoint, this is a huge mistake. It asks investors, employees, and the public to take the board’s judgment on faith.”.

The move from here, in part, is likely to attempt to bury this, David Tepper, cofounder and CEO of Ascerta, predicts.

In a recent development, “It very likely means that Nvidia will be putting out their next GPU cycle (the 6000 series) much sooner than otherwise expected,” he said via email. “They will be eager to bury the news cycle with Nvidia’s continued dominance in the space versus keeping the attention on his infidelity.”.

Nevertheless, things are not likely to be the same from here on out, said Umesh Padval, managing partner at Seligman Ventures.

It has been revealed that “No one can replace the vision he has,” said Padval. “With him back, he may not go back to 100% immediately, he’ll likely be more cautious. It will still be significantly better than a few weeks back.”.

Translation: We still can’t assume Huang will continue to be as aggressive an investor, operator, and guarantor as he may have been before, even with a supposed return to normalcy.

Sources indicate that “The private markets ecosystem has to stand by itself,” mentioned Padval. “This was driven by Nvidia a lot in the past, the whole AI ecosystem. If participation is less, the venture community needs to step it up with conviction. We all need to believe in the companies we’re backing. And if we believe in the companies, [we] don’t have to wait for the signal from Nvidia.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 19, 2026 at 9:54 amNovember 19, 2026 at 10:09 am.

Anthropic made its Nasdaq debut today in a record $81.3 billion initial public offering, with significant financial stakes for the Seattle area’s two tech giants.

Recent findings suggest that for Amazon, the IPO is a paper windfall. The organization started putting money into Anthropic in 2023, about $18 billion in all. At the $83 IPO price, its stake was worth about $161 billion. With Anthropic opening at $111.50 a share, that number was closer to $216 billion. The stock has since dropped below $100, which put Amazon’s stake under $200 billion.

Beyond the value of the investment, Anthropic is a major customer for Amazon’s cloud platform. The Claude maker has committed to spend at least $110 billion on Amazon Web Services through 2036.

According to recent reports, for Microsoft, it’s more complicated. The Redmond company agreed in late 2025 to invest up to $5 billion but hasn’t disclosed the size of its stake. Microsoft is buying $1 billion of Anthropic stock alongside the IPO, one of seven tech companies buying a combined $26 billion. Anthropic has committed to spend at least $47 billion on Microsoft’s Azure cloud through 2033.

But Microsoft is also pitching its own AI models against Anthropic’s, and it has been working to replace Anthropic’s models with OpenAI’s in some Copilot features, The Information reported this week.

Recent findings suggest that listing Anthropic’s compute partners on CNBC this morning, co-founder Daniela Amodei named Nvidia, Amazon, Google and Broadcom, but not Microsoft. Whether it was a slip or something more significant, it was an interesting omission.

A historic debut: The offering tops SpaceX’s $75 billion IPO in June, and it makes Anthropic the first standalone AI lab to go public, ahead of OpenAI.

It has been revealed that the five-year-old firm was valued at about $1.5 trillion at the $83 IPO price, on a fully diluted basis that counts employee stock and other shares not yet issued. The stock opened at $111.50, valuing Anthropic at about $2 trillion on the same basis. It has since traded as low as about $95.

Speaking before the opening bell, CEO Dario Amodei noted Anthropic will slow the training and release of its AI models for as long as it takes to be confident they’re safe, and that going public only strengthens that resolve.

“We will not bend to either business nor political pressure,” he remarked.

In an interview with CNBC’s Andrew Ross Sorkin afterward, Amodei called the push and pull between growth and that kind of restraint “one of the central tensions at the heart of the organization.”.

Anthropic is also a public benefit corporation, a structure that legally requires the tech giant to balance shareholders’ interests with the public good.

Recent findings suggest that what’s next: Both Seattle-area giants have hedged their bets. Microsoft owns about 24% of OpenAI, and Amazon put $50 billion into OpenAI earlier this year.

OpenAI, which confidentially filed for its own IPO in June, is still aiming to go public in 2027.

Anthropic’s co-founders and some of its biggest shareholders are barred from selling for up to a year under the IPO’s lock-up rules, and Amazon has said it expects a customary lock-up period.

Amazon will update the value of its Anthropic holdings in its fourth-quarter results, much of it through earnings, which means the paper windfall is likely to boost Amazon’s fourth-quarter profit even though it hasn’t sold a share.

Latest Update: AI Is Accelerating Software Development — But Businesses Need a Better Way to Measure the Quality of What They Ship

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.
  • For the last decade, the way engineering performance has been reported to leadership has followed a stable pattern.
  • Sources indicate that by 2027, the boards of software companies will be asking a different question.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

For the last decade, the way engineering performance has been reported to leadership has followed a stable pattern. Some version of the four DORA metrics — deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate and time to restore — has anchored the conversation. Engineering leaders track them. Finance leaders learn to read them. Boards nod at them.

That pattern is about to break.

Sources indicate that by 2027, the boards of software companies will be asking a different question. The question will not be “how fast are we deploying?” It will be “how much of what we deploy is actually verified?” And the reason for the shift is not fashion. It is that AI-assisted development has made the current metrics quietly unreliable, and the market is waking up to it.

Two major datasets show how far the dashboard has drifted from reality:.

In a recent development, on a typical board dashboard, the throughput gains appear as headline numbers while the instability sits in a footnote. A director reading deployment frequency would see an organization getting faster, with no view of the review process thinning out underneath it.

Recent findings suggest that DORA has acknowledged the gap. Its researchers introduced deployment rework rate, the proportion of deployments that are unplanned fixes, as a fifth measure in 2024. DORA’s Nathen Harvey stated on DX’s Engineering Enablement podcast that the four keys aren’t sufficient on their own for understanding AI’s impact.

It has been revealed that rework rate is worth tracking, but it records the fix only after a customer has already hit the bug. It can’t warn you before a release.

Code coverage reports how much of a codebase some test executed. It says nothing about whether that test checked an outcome a customer cares about, and AI-generated test suites can push coverage up without improving that second question.

A suite can touch every branch of a checkout service and still never confirm that a customer paying in a second currency gets charged the right amount.

You build verification coverage from the customer side. Product, engineering and finance agree on the journeys that make or lose money: signup, checkout, the core action the product exists for and the permission flows enterprise buyers probe during procurement.

Each journey gets an expected outcome written in business terms, such as an order confirmed at the correct price or an invited user landing with the right role. For each release, the team records how many of those journeys it ran end to end on the release candidate, in real browsers and devices, and how many produced that outcome.

A CFO can read the result without a glossary: something like “47 of 52 revenue-critical journeys verified before release.” Because your team measures it before anything ships, it should move ahead of rework rate and change failure rate, which register problems only after customers find them.

Recent findings suggest that part of the pressure comes from outside engineering. Cyber underwriters have started asking CFOs how they are managing AI risk.

In a recent development, directors who signed off on AI tooling budgets will also start asking what the spend bought besides volume. A rising deployment count tells them the team ships more often. Verification coverage tells them whether the product customers pay for still works.

Most teams can produce a first figure within a quarter by following four steps:.

Agentic test automation platforms such as KaneAI now let teams run these journeys against the rendered product on every release candidate.

DORA metrics still belong on the dashboard, because they tell you how fast and how steadily your organization delivers. Add verification coverage beside them in your next monthly report, and protect it from the pressure every board metric attracts.

A team under pressure can raise its score by shortening the journey list. Require product and finance sign-off before anyone changes it, and show the list size next to the ratio.

Include the failure cases customers hit, such as a declined card or an expired session, because a journey verified only on its happy path tells the board less than the number suggests.

Expect the score to sit below 100%, and tell directors which journeys failed and why. When they ask what AI has changed, you can show them how much of what shipped was verified to work.

For the last decade, the way engineering performance has been reported to leadership has followed a stable pattern. Some version of the four DORA metrics — deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate and time to restore — has anchored the conversation. Engineering leaders track them. Finance leaders learn to read them. Boards nod at them.

That pattern is about to break.

By 2027, the boards of software companies will be asking a different question. The question will not be “how fast are we deploying?” It will be “how much of what we deploy is actually verified?” And the reason for the shift is not fashion. It is that AI-assisted development has made the current metrics quietly unreliable, and the market is waking up to it.

#99474. The 11 days that brought Jensen Huang back to Nvidia

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1618 w)

The 11 days that brought Jensen Huang back to Nvidia

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1618 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fortune

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Last Wednesday, Elon Musk, appearing as flustered as ever, called Nvidia’s decision to push out founder Jensen Huang a huge mistake, comparing it to the Chicago Bulls dumping Michael Jordan during a winning streak.
  • It has been revealed that “There’s no one that can really replace Jensen.
  • Five days later, Musk was posting on X, the social media platform he owns, to celebrate Huang’s return.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Last Wednesday, Elon Musk, appearing as flustered as ever, called Nvidia’s decision to push out founder Jensen Huang a huge mistake, comparing it to the Chicago Bulls dumping Michael Jordan during a winning streak.

It has been revealed that “There’s no one that can really replace Jensen. He does the roles of several people,” Musk told the New York Times‘ Andrew Ross Sorkin, appearing at the newspaper’s DealBook summit via videoconference while Musk was in China with President Trump. “He has long-term relationships that have been built up over decades. He understands the technology incredibly well.”.

Five days later, Musk was posting on X, the social media platform he owns, to celebrate Huang’s return.

“It is done,” he wrote. “The mistake has been corrected.”.

Sources indicate that musk’s reaction reflects the extraordinary political muscle that he and other powerful figures in Silicon Valley and Washington flexed to bring Huang back. The Nvidia board reinstated Huang as CEO, the manufacturer confirmed Monday. His ouster, initially triggered by an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, has gripped the business and political worlds for the past two weeks, and his return promises more shockwaves in the tech industry and the halls of power. Since Huang’s resignation was announced on Nov. 12, influential figures, from Musk to Trump, have waged a pressure campaign to make Huang CEO again, even as Nvidia’s board mentioned it had moved on. Trump even called the board as it deliberated Huang’s reinstatement to push for his return.

The reversal caps one of the most remarkable resurgences in business history, while raising numerous questions about how the company moves forward, given an internal investigation into Huang and a reported probe into Nvidia’s accounting by the Securities and Exchange Commission.

This is a reconstruction of Huang’s ouster and return as it unfolded over a momentous 11-day period:.

Industry observers note that on Oct. 29, the Latest York Times reported that U.S. intelligence officials had concluded that Alice Huang (no relation), an executive at Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed, was passing information to the Chinese government, and that she had a close relationship with Jensen Huang. The Times also reported that Trump was briefed roughly a year earlier but didn’t act. Subsequent reporting detailed that China’s Ministry of State Security recruited Alice Huang to gather intelligence on Nvidia’s CEO and possibly lobby for the sale of advanced chips to China.

After the Times report, Huang told Bloomberg News there was nothing unusual about his relationship with Alice Huang, likening it to his dealings with Chinese customers and executives.

“It was all completely normal and not unusual,” he stated.

On Nov. 8, Huang publicly admitted to an affair, writing that “there is no excuse for what I did” and pledging to cooperate fully with Nvidia’s investigation, which the board declared the same day. The board, overseen by independent directors with outside counsel, said it had “no reason to believe” national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised. The next day, Chinese officials dismissed the spying claims as “pure fabrication out of thin air.”.

Recent findings suggest that on Nov. 10, the independent directors hired Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to run the investigation. The tech news website The Information reported that Alice Huang’s network had built companies to buy Nvidia chips, helping arrange about $7.5 billion in purchases, including of banned chips.

The next day, the Times reported, citing five people who worked at Nvidia, that Huang had an affair with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of health care, who has reported directly to him. Reached by phone, Huang told the Times, “I don’t think you should be talking to me directly” and hung up. Later that day, the Wall Street Journal reported that Nvidia’s 10-member board was preparing to push Huang out and had called an emergency meeting. The alleged affair with Powell violated the firm’s code of conduct, and Huang’s earlier assurances appeared to be false.

By the next morning, Nvidia confirmed Huang had resigned. Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress became interim CEO, and tech entrepreneur Harvey Jones was named Nvidia’s first board chair. The same day, Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.) and Rep. Richard E. Neal (D-Mass.) announced an inquiry into the administration’s approval of Nvidia’s H200 chip sales to China. Sen. Tim Scott (R-S.C.) asked Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to testify.

Hours after the resignation, Reuters reported, citing two people familiar with the matter, that Huang had an intimate relationship with a second, unnamed Nvidia employee. It also reported that Huang misled Nvidia General Counsel Tim Teter and Chief Marketing Officer Alison Wagonfeld in both fall 2025 and October 2026.

Nvidia shares plunged as much as 14.35% in intraday trading, wiping out about $600 billion in value at the low, and ultimately closed down 4.34%.

It has been revealed that almost as soon as Huang was ousted, a comeback effort took shape among tech and political elites and Nvidia’s own staff. A week ago, President Trump told reporters he would support reinstating Huang. “I would certainly not mind seeing that,” Trump said, adding that Huang had “learned a substantial lesson.”.

Industry observers note that an Nvidia employee debuted a website with an open letter demanding that the board reinstate Huang. As of Monday, more than 206,000 names appeared on the letter. Signatories included Musk, Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick, Shopify CEO Tobias Lutke, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney and tech investor Gavin Baker.

The day after Huang resigned, Baker and Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner mentioned in an open letter that Huang “has earned the right for a deliberate process that avoids any needless rush to replace him before all the facts are known.”.

The same day, Nvidia’s board released a statement saying it was hiring an executive search firm and hadn’t yet approached any potential candidates.

Last Tuesday, Huang broke his silence, posting on X that he was sorry for “serious mistakes” in his personal life and pledging to cooperate with the board’s investigation.

“If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the manufacturer, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” Huang wrote.

According to recent reports, the same day, Nvidia reported blockbuster earnings, with revenue of $115.8 billion, up 103%. Interim CEO Kress said the “roadmap is on track” and that Nvidia had stopped shipping AI chips to China. Jones, the board chair, said the board “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO” and that Heidrick & Struggles was running the search for the next chief executive. Nvidia also created a board committee on national security and export controls, chaired by Suzanne Nora Johnson.

Industry observers note that later that day, the Journal reported that the SEC is investigating Nvidia, including whether its disclosures misled investors. On Thursday, California Attorney General Rob Bonta subpoenaed Nvidia, seeking answers on whether China received chips or confidential information and whether investors were misled. The next day, the Times reported that Huang routinely humiliated employees, with violent threats and settlements. His spokesperson denied one fired employee’s allegations.

Last week, the S&P 500 tumbled 8.6%, its worst week since April 2025. The Nasdaq sank about 10% and the Dow 8%, the Nasdaq’s worst week since March 2020. The selloff reflected broader concerns about the AI industry, which came amid Anthropic’s initial public offering on Thursday and post-midterm-election selling, as well as investors treating Huang as a stand-in for the AI trade.

Throughout the week, tech leaders kept praising Huang and urging his return.

At a Tuesday roundtable in San Francisco that included Fortune, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella hailed Huang as “a singular person” who has contributed immensely to the tech industry, and stated it was up to Nvidia’s board to decide what happened next. On Wednesday, Anduril founder Palmer Luckey called for Huang to return during the Times‘ DealBook summit, saying that getting rid of Huang only benefited China.

In a recent development, on Sunday, Trump posted on Truth Social calling for Huang to be rehired. On Monday, Trump told CNBC he had been talking with the board and Huang, and that the board had been reasonable.

Industry observers note that “I believe my intervention was very notable,” Trump stated, adding that the U.S. national security team doesn’t believe Huang is a national security threat. Trump said he worked with Vice President JD Vance and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent to get Huang back. According to Semafor, Trump actually dialed in to the board meeting on Sunday in which the decision was made to bring Huang back. White House communications director Steven Cheung told Fortune that Trump was “totally involved.”.

Although Huang is back as CEO, the Commerce Department Monday added Megaspeed to a blacklist that will bar it from receiving Nvidia chips without having a government license.

Huang appeared at Nvidia’s Santa Clara, Calif. headquarters on Monday soon after his reinstatement was announced.

In a recent development, “Thank you all for a second chance,” he stated to a room full of employees, many cheering. “I’m going to be a better CEO the second time around.”.

By the close of markets, the S&P 500 had gained 4.7% and the Nasdaq 6.5%, the best day for both since April 2025. The recovery gained back roughly half of the S&P’s losses from last week and more than half of the Nasdaq’s. Nvidia shares rose more than 30%, to close at $165.05.

Industry observers note that on Truth Social, Trump posted an altered image that put Huang’s face on the famous photo of Trump raising his fist after the 2024 assassination attempt. In the doctored image, Huang is holding a red bra.

Uncommon Thinkers: Andrew Redd’s audacious blueprint to turn ocean volcanoes into power plants

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 19, 2026 at 10:07 amNovember 19, 2026 at 4:42 pm.
  • Recent findings suggest that editor’s note: This series profiles five Seattle-area “Uncommon Thinkers,” who will be recognized Dec.
  • Andrew Redd‘s career path creates a tidy narrative: grow up in Seattle steeped in aviation and maritime culture, study mechanical engineering and aerospace, work at SpaceX, then launch an offshore geothermal energy startup.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 19, 2026 at 10:07 amNovember 19, 2026 at 4:42 pm.

Recent findings suggest that editor’s note: This series profiles five Seattle-area “Uncommon Thinkers,” who will be recognized Dec. 10 at the GeekWire Gala in partnership with Greater Seattle Partners.

Andrew Redd‘s career path creates a tidy narrative: grow up in Seattle steeped in aviation and maritime culture, study mechanical engineering and aerospace, work at SpaceX, then launch an offshore geothermal energy startup.

The dots connect, but the picture they form is anything but ordinary: bold in vision, fast in execution and enormous in potential.

Redd has next-level ambition, and he’s directing it at solving one of the world’s biggest and most urgent problems — adding renewable, massively scalable energy that can outcompete fossil fuels and reach the grid quickly enough to make a difference in the race against climate change.

Underwater geothermal energy has never been tapped in a significant way, but to Redd, the idea was irresistible. “It checks all of the boxes for our perfect future energy source,” he stated.

It has been revealed that he founded Endurance Energy on the north shore of Seattle’s Lake Union in January 2025, and this September the team oversaw its fifth deep-sea deployment. At a site 300 miles off the Oregon coast, its prototype system generated more electricity than it consumed. The startup has raised $63 million from investors and has roughly three dozen employees.

Industry observers note that nate Bek, a principal at Ascend, praised Redd’s ability to attract “brilliant” talent in pursuit of his goal. The Seattle venture firm is one of the startup’s early backers.

It has been revealed that “I’ve been deeply inspired by what [Redd]’s building at Endurance and haven’t shut up about it since the day we met,” Bek stated. “He somehow makes powering the world from the bottom of the ocean feel inevitable, all while remaining remarkably measured and transparent about the progress.”.

Sources indicate that for Redd, studying engineering and aerospace in college was so clear-cut that it wasn’t a choice at all. Growing up around Boeing, seaplanes, the Museum of Flight and the Pacific Northwest’s rich maritime industry naturally pointed him toward those sectors. He wanted a degree as expansive as his influences.

In a recent development, “I didn’t really want to have to choose whether it was going to be boats or space travel or airplanes,” he noted. “I just wanted to be able to do anything — keep the world as wide open as possible.”.

After graduating from Princeton University, Redd worked at Neuralink, an Elon Musk firm developing technology that lets the brain communicate directly with computers. A year later, in 2021, he moved to Musk’s rocket company, SpaceX.

That was another no-duh decision, as Redd viewed it.

According to recent reports, “I saw SpaceX as really the place to be, where early-career people are given the most amount of resources and responsibility, and that felt like the fastest way to learn and the most engaging possible scenario to be in,” Redd noted. “I wanted to be tossed into something that was a little bit crazy.”.

It has been revealed that redd joined as SpaceX was starting to build its first orbital Starship rockets. The program brought together passionate young people and experienced SpaceX engineers who served as mentors. Wild ideas were entertained and explored. Everyone was committed to the mission. It was just the experience Redd wanted, and he planned to stick around for seven to 10 years.

Then artificial intelligence started booming.

In 2024, the build-out of sprawling, energy-hungry data centers for AI was accelerating with no end in sight. At the same time, efforts to electrify transportation, heating and cooling were driving up demand for power. Redd saw these trends sparking a surge in upcoming natural gas generation, locking in decades of carbon emissions.

It has been revealed that he wanted to find a better way. He went into engineering mode, focusing on all the essential criteria for an energy source: it had to be clean, not dependent on intermittent sun or wind, capable of producing massive amounts of energy, readily deployable, subject to fewer regulatory hurdles than something like nuclear, economically competitive, and scalable.

Redd recognized the tremendous heat contained under Earth’s surface as a terrific source for renewable energy and realized that most of the world’s active volcanoes are offshore. The unknown was whether the rocky ocean floor would be suitable for geothermal wells, so he did some research and found publications from geology experts who said the conditions would be “perfect.”.

“You can tell,” he mentioned, “when there’s a moment in time that you need to go and reach out and grab something, and that was really my impression — if I didn’t start this now, this would never come into existence, or wouldn’t come into existence soon enough to make a meaningful impact.”.

In launching Endurance, Redd was intentional about the culture he wanted to create. He was aiming for a multidisciplinary group of mission-driven employees eager to collaborate and learn from each other: top talent that would attract more of the same and make Endurance a place people were excited to work.

“The hardest part of an early-stage startup is recruiting,” Redd said, “especially if you’re a first-time founder.”.

The startup employs about a dozen SpaceX alumni, plus employees from the fusion company Helion Energy and the aerospace venture Blue Origin.

A strong team is key to Endurance’s success. That’s because, enthusiasm and passion aside, the startup faces steep engineering and economic challenges. The technology must withstand high pressure, corrosive conditions and mineral scaling inside devices, and seafloor machinery could be costly to repair. The systems will need expensive subsea cables to carry power to shore over potentially long distances. It’s a heavy lift.

While the September sea trial didn’t go perfectly, Redd is happy with the results. The manufacturer landed its 3-ton power plant on the seafloor near a natural vent and produced net energy from it — albeit for only 8.7 seconds. Technical difficulties and a power-cable failure cut the dive short.

Team members successfully operated the system remotely from Seattle through a fiber-optic network running along the seabed. Redd mentioned he’s grateful for access to the network, which is part of the National Science Foundation’s Regional Cabled Array and operated by the University of Washington.

Recent findings suggest that endurance engineers also drilled what they called the world’s first subsea geothermal well at a site about 5,000 feet below the ocean’s surface. The 2-inch-wide, 52-foot-deep well delivered hydrothermal fluid, but the flow was too restricted to run the power plant, sending the team to the natural vent.

Redd said there’s a lot of work ahead, but the team “made huge strides” in learning and in reducing the project’s risks.

The tech giant now is developing Leopard, its 2-megawatt generator. After testing the technology at the research site off the Oregon coast, Endurance aims to deliver power from a Leopard system in Tonga next year as its first commercial project. Subsea geothermal energy could ultimately reduce the island nation’s reliance on imported diesel and put the startup one step closer to its objective of generating terawatts of planet-friendly energy.

“This was always the end goal,” Redd stated. “Create something that is highly meaningful for the world.”.

Editor’s Note: Nate Bek of Ascend is a former GeekWire reporter.

Although XRP is at risk of losing its top-four position in the global cryptocurrency market, the asset still ranks among the three largest crypto assets in Japan.

In a recent post shared by the renowned Ripple-backed XRP treasury firm Evernorth, the organization highlighted XRP’s growing performance in the Japan crypto market.

Earlier today, Evernorth shared monthly data from the Japan Virtual and Crypto Assets Exchange Association (JVCEA) revealing that XRP recorded about ¥132.8 billion in spot trading volume in September 2026.

While this accounted for about 15% of Japan's total crypto spot trading volume during the month, XRP emerged as the third most-traded cryptocurrency in Japan after Bitcoin and Ethereum.

This shows that XRP has outperformed other major altcoins that are at the moment trading in the Japan crypto market, hitting about $880 million in trading volume.

While further data showed Solana and Dogecoin ranking next to XRP on the list as the fourth- and fifth-largest cryptocurrencies in Japan, respectively, the data also showed a wide gap from XRP’s ¥132.8 billion spot volume.

This means that XRP is significantly ahead of Solana and Dogecoin in the Japan crypto trading market, as Solana recorded only about ¥19.47 billion in trading volume during the same month.

Dogecoin, on the other hand, saw less participation, as it recorded only ¥11.27 billion in spot volume during the same period.

With XRP sitting in the third spot, the asset has become one of the most actively traded cryptocurrencies in Japan despite its persistent price volatility.

#99471. 5 Powerful Lessons Leaders Can Learn From People Who Pay It Forward

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1265 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Entrepreneur ↗ Open Full Page

5 Powerful Lessons Leaders Can Learn From People Who Pay It Forward

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1265 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Entrepreneur

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.
  • Sources indicate that when my grandmother died, people came to her funeral with stories our family had never heard.
  • Industry observers note that I founded the William S.D.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Sources indicate that when my grandmother died, people came to her funeral with stories our family had never heard. She had quietly helped them for years, asking for nothing in return. It was my first lesson in how far generosity can travel, and how much of its impact goes unrecorded.

Industry observers note that I founded the William S.D. Louey Educational Foundation in 1995 with that lesson in mind. Over the next three decades, I watched scholars build careers, support families and, in many cases, create opportunities for others. This year, the Foundation sought to understand those outcomes more systematically. It surveyed and interviewed former scholars, publishing its findings in a white paper, Opening Doors Through Education. The Foundation-led study offers an early assessment of the longer-term outcomes of its scholarship program.

The findings offer an encouraging picture of how educational opportunities can influence lives well beyond the classroom. Former scholars described how their education helped them build careers, improve their families’ circumstances and contribute to their communities. Many have also gone on to support others through mentoring, volunteering and philanthropy, extending the benefits of their education to people they may never have reached otherwise.

While the research is exploratory and cannot establish cause and effect, it raises questions that extend well beyond philanthropy. Every organization invests in people, yet few measure what those investments make possible over a lifetime. Here are five lessons I believe leaders can take from our experience.

It has been revealed that the paper introduces a measure called the William Louey Effect: the difference between the path a scholar actually followed and the one that might reasonably have been expected given their starting circumstances. The name matters less than the question behind it: compared with what?

Industry observers note that businesses regularly celebrate employees who complete leadership programs and subsequently earn promotions. But would those employees have succeeded without the training? A talented person who was already destined to thrive tells us relatively little about the program. Someone whose trajectory genuinely changed tells us considerably more.

In a recent development, leaders should examine starting circumstances, not simply final achievements. Otherwise, they risk rewarding programs for identifying talent rather than developing it.

Industry observers note that one of our paper’s most striking findings is also among its most uncertain. It estimates that parental income is approximately 46% less predictive of our scholars’ adult earnings than it is nationally in China, comparing coefficients of 0.27 and 0.50. But that estimate draws on income ranges reported by roughly 10 people, all originally selected for academic promise. Some of the difference might have existed without our support.

According to recent reports, the same problem affects corporate high-potential programs. When participants outperform their peers, how much credit belongs to the program, and how much to the selection process? Good measurement requires intellectual humility. Leaders should distinguish between outcomes they observe and impact they can reasonably attribute to their intervention. Acknowledging uncertainty does not weaken a success story. It makes the conclusions more credible.

In a recent development, from the beginning, I encouraged scholars to pay their opportunities forward when they felt ready, whether through money, knowledge or time. I never wanted that expectation to become a condition of receiving support. The paper calls this voluntary reciprocity: giving that emerges from gratitude and personal conviction rather than contractual obligation.

It has been revealed that organizations often seek loyalty through retention bonuses, repayment clauses and restrictive agreements. Such mechanisms can serve legitimate purposes, but they cannot manufacture genuine commitment. Some of our earliest scholars independently established and funded a scholarship for Chinese students at Oxford. We did not require them to do so, because when people feel trusted rather than indebted, they have the freedom to turn an opportunity they received into something of their own.

Recent findings suggest that generosity becomes more powerful when people can see what it looks like. Several scholars who established the Oxford scholarship also mentor its recipients, offering guidance similar to the support they once received. They are passing forward not only financial resources, but a way of treating people.

Industry observers note that the leadership lesson is practical. If you want employees to mentor colleagues, share knowledge and create opportunities, make those expectations visible through your own behavior. Take time to advise younger employees, introduce promising people to contacts who can help them, and continue supporting colleagues even when there is no immediate benefit to you. Then give others the freedom to contribute in their own ways.

A culture of generosity cannot be built through instructions alone. It grows when people repeatedly experience the behavior their leaders advocate.

Sources indicate that we have never asked a scholar to repay their scholarship. Instead, many have supported relatives, mentored students or helped others pursue opportunities. One former scholar described the experience as bringing philanthropy forward by a generation. For business leaders, this suggests a broader definition of return on investment.

Recent findings suggest that consider an employee who leaves your firm and becomes an exceptional manager elsewhere, or a former trainee who mentors people you will never meet. Your organization may receive no direct financial benefit, yet its investment continues producing value. Traditional performance dashboards rarely capture that contribution.

It has been revealed that our paper argues that measuring educational outcomes only at graduation or the first job can overlook changes that emerge much later, including leadership, entrepreneurship and upward mobility. The same applies to professional development. A program evaluated after 12 months may reveal little about the influence its participants eventually have on others. Leaders should consider staying connected with former employees and tracking how their contributions evolve, without treating their subsequent achievements as corporate property.

According to recent reports, the Foundation offers its framework as a starting point, not a definitive answer. We hope other scholarship providers and universities will test it with larger groups and more rigorous comparisons. Business leaders need not adopt our terminology to apply the underlying principle.

When deciding whether an investment in people has succeeded, ask two questions: What did this person achieve, and what did they subsequently make possible for others? The second is harder to measure, and its benefits may never return directly to the organization that made the investment. But three decades after founding the Foundation, I have come to believe it may be the more important question.

When my grandmother died, people came to her funeral with stories our family had never heard. She had quietly helped them for years, asking for nothing in return. It was my first lesson in how far generosity can travel, and how much of its impact goes unrecorded.

In a recent development, I founded the William S.D. Louey Educational Foundation in 1995 with that lesson in mind. Over the next three decades, I watched scholars build careers, support families and, in many cases, create opportunities for others. This year, the Foundation sought to understand those outcomes more systematically. It surveyed and interviewed former scholars, publishing its findings in a white paper, Opening Doors Through Education. The Foundation-led study offers an early assessment of the longer-term outcomes of its scholarship program.

The findings offer an encouraging picture of how educational opportunities can influence lives well beyond the classroom. Former scholars described how their education helped them build careers, improve their families’ circumstances and contribute to their communities. Many have also gone on to support others through mentoring, volunteering and philanthropy, extending the benefits of their education to people they may never have reached otherwise.
